# Traffic Monitor

> Open-source roadway counting and speed monitoring on a Raspberry Pi

The Traffic Monitor turns a Raspberry Pi 5 with a camera, Doppler radar, and an optional AI accelerator into an open source roadway counter and speed monitor. These docs cover hardware, installation, setup, configuration, the on-device dashboards, and data payloads.

# Get started

# Traffic Monitor docs

[Traffic Monitor](https://www.trafficmonitor.ai/) is open source software that turns a Raspberry Pi 5 with a camera and a Doppler radar into a roadway counter and speed monitor. It counts pedestrians, bicycles, and vehicles, measures vehicle speeds, and keeps the data on the device.

Be counted

Privacy is part of the design. Object detection runs on the device, the database records labels, speeds, and times rather than people, and nothing is sent to an outside server unless you set it up. [Data and privacy](https://docs.trafficmonitor.ai/dev/data-and-payloads/data-overview/index.md) lists what the device stores, including the short-lived snapshots and clips that Frigate keeps by default, and who on your network can see them.

Our mission is to democratize the power of AI tools to improve community safety and quality of life, through the ethical and transparent use of these capabilities.

# How it works

A Traffic Monitor is a Raspberry Pi 5 running a few cooperating programs. Everything happens on the device, so it works without an internet connection once it's installed.

## From the street to the database

1. **The camera** streams H.265 video at 1536×864 and 10 frames per second to Frigate.

1. **[Frigate](https://frigate.video/)** finds and tracks objects in the video, using the AI accelerator if the device has one and the CPU if not. It records which **zones** each object passed through. When an object leaves the frame, Frigate publishes an event on the device's MQTT broker.

1. **The radar** (optional) measures the speed and direction of whatever moves in front of it and reports readings over USB several times a second.

1. **[Node-RED](https://nodered.org/)** runs the Traffic Monitor logic. It keeps every radar reading, and it records every moving object from an enabled camera as an event. When the camera has a radar and the object entered any zone, it:

   - works out the direction of travel from the order in which the object entered `zone_near` and `zone_far`, or from the radar if the zones don't give one;
   - attaches a speed: the median radar reading in that direction while the object was in view, with a two-second margin on each side.

   Without a radar, events have no direction or speed. [Direction and speed](https://docs.trafficmonitor.ai/dev/data-and-payloads/events-payload/#direction-and-speed) has the exact rules.

   The dashboards and the daily counts then filter the events by zone: they count objects that passed through `zone_capture`, and they use only objects that passed through `zone_radar` for speed statistics. 5. **The database**, one SQLite file on the device, stores the events, the radar readings, air quality readings from the optional sensor, and the device's deployment history. The dashboards read from it, and you can download it.

[First-time setup](https://docs.trafficmonitor.ai/dev/setup-guide/index.md) walks through turning on detection and adjusting the four zones. [Events](https://docs.trafficmonitor.ai/dev/data-and-payloads/events-payload/index.md) lists every column an event has.

## What you see

The device serves a home page at `http://<device>/` that links to the dashboards, Frigate, and the system tools. [Home page and apps](https://docs.trafficmonitor.ai/dev/use/home-page/index.md) describes each one.

## What stays on the device

The database holds labels, times, speeds, and zones, not pictures. Frigate keeps cropped snapshots and short clips for about an hour so you can check what was detected, and nothing is sent anywhere unless you turn on an integration. [Data and privacy](https://docs.trafficmonitor.ai/dev/data-and-payloads/data-overview/index.md) has the details.

## Settings

Three files on the device control the behavior described above. You edit them over SSH.

| File                    | What it controls                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                           |
| ----------------------- | ------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------ |
| Frigate's `config.yml`  | Camera, detection, zones, object filters, and recording. Most changes are made in Frigate's own web UI. See [Tune object detection](https://docs.trafficmonitor.ai/dev/configuration/frigate-config/index.md).                                                                                                                                                                                                                             |
| Node-RED's `config.yml` | Deployment location, which sensors are on, which radar pairs with which camera, and the ThingsBoard connection. Times shown on the dashboards use the device's time zone, which the installer sets and the control app's [Date and time](https://docs.trafficmonitor.ai/dev/use/device-health/#the-date-and-time-page) page changes. See [config.yml settings](https://docs.trafficmonitor.ai/dev/configuration/node-red-config/index.md). |
| `node-red-tm.env`       | Radar serial ports, the database path, and the MQTT broker. See [node-red-tm.env settings](https://docs.trafficmonitor.ai/dev/configuration/environment/#node-red-tmenv).                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                  |

# Choose your path

## 1. Get a Traffic Monitor

- **[Build your own](https://docs.trafficmonitor.ai/dev/build-your-own-device-diy/index.md)**

  ______________________________________________________________________

  Buy the [hardware](https://docs.trafficmonitor.ai/dev/build-your-own-device-diy/recommended-hardware/index.md), [assemble](https://docs.trafficmonitor.ai/dev/build-your-own-device-diy/assembly-instructions/index.md) it, and [install the software](https://docs.trafficmonitor.ai/dev/software-installation/index.md). The software is open source and the parts are sold at retail.

- **Start with a pre-built unit**

  ______________________________________________________________________

  The software is installed. Skip to step 2, and ask your provider how the unit connects to your network.

## 2. Deploy it

The device needs a clear view of the roadway, and the radar needs a shallow angle to the direction of travel. [Choose a site and mount](https://docs.trafficmonitor.ai/dev/deployment-and-mounting-guide/index.md) covers both, for [temporary](https://docs.trafficmonitor.ai/dev/deployment-and-mounting-guide/#temporary-deployments) and [permanent](https://docs.trafficmonitor.ai/dev/deployment-and-mounting-guide/#permanent-deployments) deployments.

## 3. Set it up

Power it on and follow [First-time setup](https://docs.trafficmonitor.ai/dev/setup-guide/index.md): open the home page, turn on detection, adjust the zones to your roadway, and record the device's location. This takes about half an hour.

## 4. Use the data

The device counts around the clock and starts again by itself after a power cut. Watch the [Monitoring dashboard](https://docs.trafficmonitor.ai/dev/ui/monitoring/index.md), review detections in Frigate, [export the data](https://docs.trafficmonitor.ai/dev/ui/database/index.md), or send it to [ThingsBoard](https://docs.trafficmonitor.ai/dev/data-and-payloads/integrations/index.md).

Some operators pair the device with a display that shows the day's counts. Share what you build in [Show and tell](https://github.com/glossyio/traffic-monitor/discussions/new?category=show-and-tell) or on the [Zulip chat](https://trafficmonitor.zulipchat.com/).

LED display showing daily counts from a Traffic Monitor
# Build your own

# Build your own

A Traffic Monitor is a Raspberry Pi 5, a camera, an optional radar and AI accelerator, and a weather-resistant enclosure. Building one takes an afternoon.

1. [Hardware](https://docs.trafficmonitor.ai/dev/build-your-own-device-diy/recommended-hardware/index.md): the parts list, with the options that have been tested.
1. [Assembly](https://docs.trafficmonitor.ai/dev/build-your-own-device-diy/assembly-instructions/index.md): fitting the parts into the 3D-printed enclosure.
1. [Install the software](https://docs.trafficmonitor.ai/dev/software-installation/index.md): image the microSD card and run the installer.
1. [Update the software](https://docs.trafficmonitor.ai/dev/build-your-own-device-diy/update/index.md): when a new release comes out.

Then continue with [Choose a site and mount](https://docs.trafficmonitor.ai/dev/deployment-and-mounting-guide/index.md) and [First-time setup](https://docs.trafficmonitor.ai/dev/setup-guide/index.md).

# Assembly

These steps assume the [parts list](https://docs.trafficmonitor.ai/dev/build-your-own-device-diy/recommended-hardware/index.md) and the 3D-printed enclosure. Each numbered step matches a numbered photo.

Full set of Traffic Monitor parts ready for assembly

Steps 1 to 34 assemble the Raspberry Pi 5, Camera Module 3, AI accelerator (Coral TPU HAT or AI HAT+), and radar. Steps 35 to 51 add the optional air quality sensor.

## Core parts

1. Lay out all your parts and screws
1. Lay out all your parts and screws (double-check)
1. M3×12 mm screws for the camera, M3×6 mm for the radar, M3×10 mm for the carrier board
1. Lay out all your parts and screws
1. (Coral TPU M.2 module and HAT pictured) Unbox the AI accelerator and the M.2 board, if separate
1. (Coral TPU M.2 module and HAT pictured) Attach the M.2 module to the board and attach the ribbon cable
1. Attach the active cooler to the Raspberry Pi
1. Lay out the HAT stand-offs
1. Attach the stand-offs to the board (bottom-HAT version shown)
1. Plug in the PCIe ribbon cable. *Match the triangle marks on the ribbon cable, the Raspberry Pi, and the HAT.*
1. Attach the HAT to the Raspberry Pi (bottom HAT shown, for the Coral TPU)
1. Locate the Raspberry Pi carrier plate
1. Turn the carrier plate so the built-in stand-offs point down
1. Mount the Raspberry Pi and HAT to the carrier plate
1. Bottom of the carrier plate
1. Locate the radar and its mounting board
1. Attach the radar to the mounting board with M3×6 mm screws, with the antenna (the white and gold areas) at the bottom and the micro-USB plug near the camera cut-out
1. Locate the camera, camera mounts, and camera ribbon cable
1. If the camera came with a white ribbon cable, remove it. It doesn't fit the Raspberry Pi 5.
1. Attach the Raspberry Pi 5 camera ribbon cable to the camera
1. Slide the camera into the first camera mounting plate
1. Snap on the other camera mounting plate so all the holes and pins align
1. The camera mount stand-offs are on the back, and the first plate sits flush with the end of the stand-offs
1. Locate the main mounting board and the assembled camera mount
1. Locate four M3×12 mm screws for the camera
1. (Pictures continue below) Mount the camera in either of the camera mount holes
1. Radar and camera mounted, from the front
1. Pass the camera ribbon cable through the camera mounting hole to the back
1. Front view with the camera ribbon cable through the back
1. Locate the main mounting board, the carrier plate, and the M3×10 mm screws
1. Attach the carrier board to the main board
1. Front view with the carrier board attached
1. Plug the camera ribbon cable into either of the Raspberry Pi 5 camera connectors
1. Place the main mounting board into the enclosure, with the radar and camera at the top facing forward, and secure it with M3×10 mm screws in the four corners

## Air quality sensor

35. Locate the Enviro+ board and the particulate matter (PM) sensor
01. Unpack both
01. Attach the Enviro+ board to the PM sensor
01. Back of the Enviro+ board
01. Locate the GPIO ribbon cable
01. Attach the ribbon cable to the Enviro+ board with the wires going down and the notch on top
01. Place the PM sensor in its slot, pushed fully onto the pins in the bottom of the enclosure
01. The PM sensor from below
01. Slip the Enviro+ board into the air quality carrier board
01. Line up the pins on the bottom of the carrier board with the Enviro+ board. It may be snug.
01. Gently place the carrier board into the alignment slots in the enclosure
01. There should be almost no gap between the carrier board and the enclosure
01. Fold the ribbon cable up and tuck the PM sensor cable on top of the PM sensor
01. Slide the air quality shroud into its slots so you can see the screw inserts, and secure it with M3×8 mm screws
01. Front of the assembled sensor
01. Top of the assembled sensor
01. The assembled sensor from outside the enclosure

### Attach the GPIO ribbon cable

Attach the ribbon cable to the Raspberry Pi's GPIO pins with the notch on top.

Attach the ribbon cable with the notch toward the outside of the Raspberry Pi

- Pre-fold the cable so it lies flat when the case is closed.
- The connector is tight on the pins and close to the cooler's heatsink. Work it down a few millimeters at a time, side to side, until it's fully seated.
- To remove it, unplug the Raspberry Pi first. Slide a flat-head screwdriver between the connector and the plastic header and work the connector off a few millimeters at a time, taking care not to short the pins.

## Ready to deploy

Close the case. Next, [install the software](https://docs.trafficmonitor.ai/dev/software-installation/index.md).

Traffic Monitors ready to count

______________________________________________________________________

## description: The parts for a Traffic Monitor: Raspberry Pi 5, camera, AI accelerator, radar, enclosure, power, and the optional air quality sensor.

# Hardware

The core parts are the Raspberry Pi 5, a microSD card, a camera, and an AI accelerator. A radar adds accurate speeds, and an air quality sensor adds environmental readings. You can swap parts, but the docs and the default settings assume the parts below.

What each combination gives you:

1. **Camera and AI accelerator**: object detection and counts. The lowest cost.
1. **Add a radar** for speeds and the direction of travel. Without a radar, events have no speed or direction.
1. **Add an air quality sensor** for gases, particulate matter, temperature, pressure, humidity, and light.
1. **Add cameras** to watch more directions with the same accelerator. The software supports several cameras and up to four radars, paired in any pattern. See [Cameras](#cameras).

## Parts list

We are not affiliated with the stores or companies linked here. These are parts contributors have used or tested; if you've tested others, post in the [discussions](https://github.com/glossyio/traffic-monitor/discussions).

- Computer: [Raspberry Pi 5](https://www.raspberrypi.com/products/raspberry-pi-5/), 4 GB or 8 GB
  - Power: the official [27 W USB-C power supply](https://www.pishop.us/product/raspberry-pi-27w-usb-c-power-supply-black-us/)
  - Cooling: the [Raspberry Pi active cooler](https://www.raspberrypi.com/products/active-cooler/)
- Storage: a microSD card of 32 GB or more, such as the [Raspberry Pi SD card](https://www.raspberrypi.com/products/sd-cards/) or the [SanDisk Extreme Pro](https://www.westerndigital.com/products/memory-cards/sandisk-extreme-pro-uhs-i-microsd?sku=SDSQXCD-128G-GN6MA)
- Camera: [Raspberry Pi Camera Module 3](https://www.raspberrypi.com/products/camera-module-3/), wide angle, plus a [Raspberry Pi 5 camera cable](https://www.raspberrypi.com/products/camera-cable/)
- AI accelerator: see [AI accelerator](#ai-accelerator)
- Radar (recommended): [OmniPreSense OPS243-A](https://omnipresense.com/product/ops243-doppler-radar-sensor/)
- Enclosure: see [Enclosure](#enclosure)
- Air quality sensor (optional): [Enviro+](https://www.pishop.us/product/enviro-for-raspberry-pi/) with the [PMS5003 particulate matter sensor](https://www.pishop.us/product/pms5003-particulate-matter-sensor-with-cable/) and a [male-to-female GPIO ribbon cable](https://www.pishop.us/product/male-to-female-gpio-ribbon-cable/)
- Screws: assorted M3 for the boards and enclosure, M2.5×10 mm for the Raspberry Pi

## Computer

The [Raspberry Pi 5](https://www.raspberrypi.com/products/raspberry-pi-5/) with 4 GB of memory runs the standard setup. Choose 8 GB if you plan to add sensors or other applications. Add the [active cooler](https://www.raspberrypi.com/products/active-cooler/); it's inexpensive and prevents throttling on hot days.

Warning

The Raspberry Pi 4 and earlier can't supply enough power over USB for the accelerator and the radar together, which causes resets and dropped readings. Some people have run object detection alone on older models.

### Storage

A good microSD card of 32 GB or more holds the system and the database. Both the [Raspberry Pi SD card](https://www.raspberrypi.com/products/sd-cards/?variant=sd-64gb) and the [SanDisk Extreme Pro](https://www.westerndigital.com/products/memory-cards/sandisk-extreme-pro-uhs-i-microsd?sku=SDSQXCD-128G-GN6MA) have been tested. An NVMe (M.2) drive is faster and more durable, and some M.2 HATs hold both a drive and a Coral accelerator.

### Power

The Raspberry Pi 5 needs a 27 W supply (5 V at 5 A). A weaker supply, such as an older Raspberry Pi adapter, causes resets and throttling. The device itself draws 6 to 14 W while detecting, and every part is powered from the Raspberry Pi.

- **Mains:** the official [27 W USB-C power supply](https://www.pishop.us/product/raspberry-pi-27w-usb-c-power-supply-black-us/).
- **Power over Ethernet:** a PoE HAT such as the [Waveshare PoE HAT (F)](https://www.waveshare.com/poe-hat-f.htm) or [Waveshare PoE M.2 HAT+](https://www.waveshare.com/PoE-M.2-HAT-Plus.htm), with a PoE+ source such as the [Raspberry Pi PoE+ injector](https://www.raspberrypi.com/products/poe-plus-injector/).
- **Battery for about a day:** a portable power station such as a [Jackery Explorer 300](https://www.jackery.com/products/jackery-explorer-300-v2-portable-power-station), with the official power supply plugged into it. A 300 Wh station lasts about a day.

Longer off-grid use: custom battery and solar

**Battery.** Use a 12 V or 24 V [LiFePO₄](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lithium_iron_phosphate_battery) battery and a [buck converter](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Buck_converter) that steps it down to 5 V at 5 A. Size the battery from the device's draw of about 13 W: a 12 V, 10 Ah battery (120 Wh) lasts about 9 hours, and 24 hours needs 13 × 24 = 312 Wh, a 12 V battery of about 30 Ah.

**Solar.** Add a [photovoltaic](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Photovoltaics) panel and a [charge controller](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Charge_controller) to the battery setup. Size the panel for the worst month:

1. Look up your daily [solar potential](https://profilesolar.com/countries/US/). Portland, Oregon, gets about 7.15 kWh/day in summer and 1.42 kWh/day in winter per kW of panel.
1. Multiply by the panel size. A 100 W panel in a Portland winter produces about 1.42 × 0.1 = 142 Wh per day.
1. Allow for the controller. A PWM controller passes about 80%, so 142 × 0.8 = 113 Wh per day.
1. Compare with the 312 Wh the device uses per day. A 100 W panel isn't enough; a Portland winter needs about 300 W of panel.

Real output depends on panel angle, cloud, shade from trees, and snow. This setup is a prototype, not a tested product.

## Cameras

The [Raspberry Pi Camera Module 3](https://www.raspberrypi.com/products/camera-module-3/) in its wide-angle version is the tested camera. It needs the [Raspberry Pi 5 camera cable](https://www.raspberrypi.com/products/camera-cable/), sold separately. The [Raspberry Pi Global Shutter camera](https://www.raspberrypi.com/products/raspberry-pi-global-shutter-camera/) has been tested too, for faster motion or a custom lens, with the same cable. It needs camera stream settings that match its sensor, because the defaults are for Camera Module 3. They're in `/var/lib/go2rtc/go2rtc.yaml`, which every update replaces, so redo them after updating.

The Raspberry Pi 5 has two camera connectors, so it can take two Raspberry Pi cameras. Network cameras also work; see [Frigate's camera recommendations](https://docs.frigate.video/frigate/hardware#cameras). Choose one that streams H.265 (HEVC), which the Raspberry Pi 5 decodes in hardware. H.264 works with software decoding but costs CPU, so keep to one or two such cameras.

## AI accelerator

An AI accelerator runs the object detection model at over 100 frames per second with a few milliseconds per inference, enough for several cameras. Without one, Frigate detects on the CPU, which is slower and misses more objects on a busy road, so an accelerator is recommended for any deployment with a camera.

1. **Recommended:** [Raspberry Pi AI HAT+](https://www.raspberrypi.com/products/ai-hat/) with the Hailo-8 or Hailo-8L.
1. **Older:** [Coral USB Accelerator](https://coral.ai/products/accelerator). It has become expensive and hard to find.
1. **Older:** [Coral M.2 Accelerator B+M key](https://coral.ai/products/m2-accelerator-bm/) (not the A+E key) on the [Raspberry Pi M.2 HAT+](https://www.raspberrypi.com/products/m2-hat-plus/).

Frigate's [supported detectors](https://docs.frigate.video/configuration/object_detectors) lists other options. The installer detects the Coral and Hailo accelerators and configures Frigate for whichever it finds.

## Radar

The [OmniPreSense OPS243-A](https://omnipresense.com/product/ops243-doppler-radar-sensor/) Doppler radar measures speed and direction up to about 100 m away and is certified with the same tests as law-enforcement speed radars. It connects over USB.

## Air quality sensor

The [Enviro+](https://www.pishop.us/product/enviro-for-raspberry-pi/) board with the [PMS5003 particulate matter sensor](https://www.pishop.us/product/pms5003-particulate-matter-sensor-with-cable/) measures gases, particulates, temperature, pressure, humidity, and light. It plugs into the Raspberry Pi's GPIO header through a [male-to-female ribbon cable](https://www.pishop.us/product/male-to-female-gpio-ribbon-cable/), which reaches the sensor's place in the enclosure. [Air quality sensor](https://docs.trafficmonitor.ai/dev/add-ons/air-quality/index.md) covers the software.

## Enclosure

- **Print it.** The 3D-printable enclosure is open source at [greendormer/tm-enclosure-3d](https://github.com/greendormer/tm-enclosure-3d), with a parts list.
- **Adapt a junction box.** A waterproof electrical box of about 9 × 7 × 4 inches, such as the [TICONN IP67 ABS enclosure](https://www.amazon.com/gp/product/B0B87X944Z), holds the parts, the camera, and the radar with some modification.

# Update the software

An update reruns the installer from a newer copy of the repository. Your data and your settings stay; the containers are rebuilt.

## Before you update

- Read the [release notes](https://github.com/glossyio/traffic-monitor/releases). A release that needs a fresh image says so.
- Download a copy of the database from the [Data export](https://docs.trafficmonitor.ai/dev/ui/database/#download-the-database) page.
- Make sure the device has an internet connection. The update downloads packages and rebuilds the container images. Rebuilding Frigate's image compiles ffmpeg on the device, which can take about 20 minutes.

## Update

Connect to the device over SSH, then update the clone you installed from and rerun the whole installer:

```
cd traffic-monitor
git pull
bash script/tmsetup.sh
```

Run the whole installer rather than a single tag, because one version's changes can span several components.

Restart when the installer asks. When the services come back, the Node-RED service applies any database schema changes before it opens the database. [Schema versions](https://docs.trafficmonitor.ai/dev/data-and-payloads/data-overview/#schema-versions) describes the copy it saves first.

Every app asks for the device's login, and the Node-RED editor has no login of its own: it opens for the device's administrator. If the device has no administrator account yet, every page opens the setup page instead. Claim the device with the setup code from the end of the installer's output; until the device is claimed, `sudo cat /etc/traffic-monitor/setup-code` also shows it. [Control app and login](https://docs.trafficmonitor.ai/dev/use/control-app/index.md) walks through setup and adding accounts.

The installer printed `tm-control migrate: WARNING` or `ERROR`

The installer brings Frigate's configuration up to date, moves the ThingsBoard and Plate Recognizer tokens out of `config.yml` and the add-on's env file and a Frigate+ key out of `frigate.env`, and warns about what it can't change safely. An `ERROR` line means the installer stopped; the last item below covers the two causes. Each warning names the camera, stream, setting, or file. To find the warnings later:

```
grep -E 'tm-control migrate: (WARNING|ERROR)' ~/tmsetup-*.log
```

**A camera input or stream without a login.** A camera's input `path` in Frigate's configuration reads a stream on port 8554 without a login. If that path points at this device, for example by its IP address, add `{FRIGATE_GO2RTC_RTSP_USER}:{FRIGATE_GO2RTC_RTSP_PASSWORD}@` before the host in Frigate's configuration editor. The [higher-resolution stream](https://docs.trafficmonitor.ai/dev/configuration/frigate-config/#higher-resolution-stream) section shows a complete path. If it points at another device, leave it as it is.

**An `auth`, `proxy`, or `tls` setting.** The installer adds the settings that turn off Frigate's own login and let Frigate trust the user and role that the device's login passes on. It leaves a section that's already there as it is, and warns when a setting in it would get in the way:

- `auth.enabled` or `tls.enabled` is true or missing: Frigate asks for its own login as well as the device's, or serves its port over TLS, which the device doesn't use.
- A `proxy` setting doesn't match, followed by `auth was not added` when the file had no `auth` section: Frigate could trust user and role headers the device doesn't set, so the installer leaves Frigate's own login on.

Change each named setting to match the [default Frigate config](https://github.com/glossyio/traffic-monitor/blob/main/container/frigate/config/config.yml.j2), in `/opt/traffic-monitor/frigate/config/config.yml` over SSH. Then run `bash script/tmsetup.sh -t frigate`, which adds what's still missing, and restart Frigate with `sudo systemctl restart frigate.service`.

**A token or key that wasn't moved.** The installer moves a ThingsBoard token, a Plate Recognizer token, and a license key that it finds in `config.yml` or in `plate-recognizer.env`, and a Frigate+ key typed into `frigate.env`, to the device's secrets, and deletes the keys from `config.yml`. It leaves a value that isn't text, or that has a character a token can't have, such as a space, and warns about it. A Frigate+ key moves only in the format Frigate+ shows it in, on its own or between double quotes; for a key it leaves, the installer writes the device's own key, or none, into `frigate.env`. It also warns when a value differs from the one the device already holds. The device keeps the value it holds, and `config.yml` and the env files are backed up with a timestamp, so the other value stays in the backup. That backup's name ends in `.migrate.bak`, and it stays until you delete it. Enter the token on the control app's [Device page](https://docs.trafficmonitor.ai/dev/use/device-health/#tokens-and-keys), or the Frigate+ key on its [Detection page](https://docs.trafficmonitor.ai/dev/use/detection/#frigate-plus), and delete a key the installer left in `config.yml`.

**A file that is a symbolic link, or a YAML error (`ERROR`).** The installer refuses to change a `config.yml` or env file that is a symbolic link, and stops. Replace the link with the file itself, then run the installer again. A YAML error in Node-RED's `config.yml` also stops the installer, as one in Frigate's does. Fix the error in `/opt/traffic-monitor/node-red-tm/config/config.yml`, then run the installer again.

A Frigate configuration from a backup may lack the camera stream login and the proxy settings. After you restore one, run `bash script/tmsetup.sh -t frigate` to add them.

Port 1883 accepts MQTT connections only from the device itself unless the broker has a login. If a display board, Home Assistant, or another device on your network reads MQTT from this device, give the broker a login and give it to that device; see [Connect from other devices](https://docs.trafficmonitor.ai/dev/data-and-payloads/integrations/#connect-from-other-devices).

Open `http://<device>/`, log in, and check the [Monitoring dashboard](https://docs.trafficmonitor.ai/dev/ui/monitoring/index.md) for new counts. After an update from a version without the Location page, that first visit to the control app also sets up the device's places; see [Places after an update](#places-after-an-update).

To update several devices from your computer, use the remote form of the installer described in [Install the software](https://docs.trafficmonitor.ai/dev/software-installation/#install-from-another-computer).

## Places after an update

An update from a version without the control app's Location page brings the location settings up to date:

- The installer adds `database_precision: '2'` to `config.yml`, so the database stores the location rounded to about 1 km. It removes any `lat` and `lon` under a camera or radar, because the location belongs to the whole device, and its output names each sensor.
- When Node-RED first starts, it saves a copy of the database, gives each location in the stored rows a place id, and rounds the stored coordinates to two decimal places, once. The copy keeps the exact rows until the next update that changes the database replaces it; see [Schema versions](https://docs.trafficmonitor.ai/dev/data-and-payloads/data-overview/#schema-versions).

Then open the control app and log in, as any user. The first time its home page, Status page, or [Location page](https://docs.trafficmonitor.ai/dev/use/location/index.md) opens after Node-RED has started, the control app sets up the device's places:

- Each location in the saved copy becomes a used place, marked **Imported from your previous settings**.
- The place at the location in `config.yml` becomes the place in use, and the control app writes its id into `config.yml`, so the deployments running now carry on. If no imported place is at that location, for example because it changed while the device was off, the control app makes a new place from `config.yml`, and new deployments start.
- A device with no location in `config.yml` gets a new place in use with no location. Its past places are imported all the same.

Open the control app before the next update

The control app reads the past places from the saved copy, and the next update that changes the database replaces it. Open the control app before then, and keep the copy until the Location page lists the places. If Node-RED hasn't answered yet, the Status page's Location check says the places haven't been set up, and the control app tries again each time a page that shows the checks opens.

If there's no copy, or the control app can't read it, the control app skips the import and makes only the place in use, from `config.yml`. The past places' records stay in the database, grouped by place id, but the Location page doesn't list those places.

A device whose sensors had their own coordinates

The update gives each sensor's own location a place of its own. Once the control app writes the place in use into `config.yml`, each sensor whose location differed from the device's starts a new deployment there. Its earlier records stay with their own place, which the Location page lists as used.

## What an update changes

An update replaces the container images, service units, Node-RED flows, and the reverse proxy configuration. It keeps your settings files, the database, Frigate's recordings, and the device's accounts. With `-f`, it also replaces the settings files with fresh copies from the templates and keeps each old file beside the new one with a timestamp. [What `-f` replaces](https://docs.trafficmonitor.ai/dev/reference/tmsetup/#what-f-replaces) lists the files.

Use `-f` when a release changes the settings files and you want the new template. Afterwards, turn Frigate's detection back on and redo your settings from the timestamped copies: the `sensors` section of `config.yml`, and zones in Frigate. [First-time setup](https://docs.trafficmonitor.ai/dev/setup-guide/index.md) walks through each. You don't need to copy back `survey_id`, `lat`, `lon`, `database_precision`, or the bearings: the next time the control app is opened, it puts back the place in use, its location, the precision you chose, and the way each sensor faces there; see [Edit the location by hand](https://docs.trafficmonitor.ai/dev/configuration/node-red-config/#edit-the-location-by-hand).

Node-RED flow changes made in the editor on the device are replaced on every update. Commit them to the repository instead; see [Dev environment](https://docs.trafficmonitor.ai/dev/development/dev-environment/index.md).

## Update one component

Each installer tag reruns one component, plus anything that has to change with it; see [Tags](https://docs.trafficmonitor.ai/dev/reference/tmsetup/#tags). For example, after plugging in a radar:

```
bash script/tmsetup.sh -t node-red-tm
```

[Installer options](https://docs.trafficmonitor.ai/dev/reference/tmsetup/index.md) lists the tags and flags.

# Install the software

The Traffic Monitor runs on a Raspberry Pi 5 with Raspberry Pi OS Lite (64-bit). One installer script sets up the operating system, detects the radars and the AI accelerator, builds the containers on the device, and reboots when it needs to.

## Prepare the card

1. Open [Raspberry Pi Imager](https://www.raspberrypi.com/documentation/computers/getting-started.html#install-using-imager) on your computer, with the microSD card in a card reader.
1. Choose **Raspberry Pi OS (other) > Raspberry Pi OS Lite (64-bit)**. The full desktop image works but installs software the Traffic Monitor doesn't use.
1. In [OS customization](https://www.raspberrypi.com/documentation/computers/getting-started.html#advanced-options), set a hostname, a username and password, your Wi-Fi network, and turn on SSH. The hostname becomes the device's address on your network: `http://<hostname>.local/`.
1. Write the card, put it in the Raspberry Pi, and power it on. The first boot takes a few minutes.

## Install on the device

The device needs an internet connection during the install. Afterwards it runs offline.

Connect over SSH with the username and hostname you chose:

```
ssh <username>@<hostname>.local
```

Then download the repository and run the installer:

```
sudo apt update && sudo apt install -y git
git clone https://github.com/glossyio/traffic-monitor
bash traffic-monitor/script/tmsetup.sh
```

The installer asks for your password when it needs administrator rights. If the device has no Wi-Fi country yet, it also asks for one, as a two-letter code such as `US` or `GB`, because the device's hotspot needs it; press Enter for `US`. A first install takes 30 minutes or more. Building Frigate's container image compiles ffmpeg on the device, which alone takes about 20 minutes with little output, so leave it running.

Near the end, the installer shows the device's card on the terminal: its **setup code**, which you need once to claim the device and create its administrator account, and the name and password of its hotspot. Keep them; the hotspot's password isn't in the installer's log, and `sudo tm-control card` prints the card again. [Control app and login](https://docs.trafficmonitor.ai/dev/use/control-app/#claim-the-device) says where else to find the setup code.

Then the installer asks to reboot. A first install always needs the reboot, with or without an AI accelerator, because it changes the Raspberry Pi's boot settings for the camera and any accelerator it found. The services start after the reboot. After it, open `http://<hostname>.local/`, claim the device with the setup code, and continue with [First-time setup](https://docs.trafficmonitor.ai/dev/setup-guide/index.md). A device that isn't on a network you can reach runs its own hotspot. Join it with the password from the card, and your phone's sign-in window opens the setup page. Once the device is claimed, an administrator can put it on a Wi-Fi network from the control app's Network page; see [Wi-Fi and the hotspot](https://docs.trafficmonitor.ai/dev/use/wifi-hotspot/index.md). The Wi-Fi network you set in Imager works too, and the Network page lists it as a saved network.

The installer's flags, such as a different install folder or time zone, are listed in [Installer options](https://docs.trafficmonitor.ai/dev/reference/tmsetup/index.md).

## Install from another computer

The same script can install or update one or more devices over SSH from a Linux or Mac computer. Each device needs Raspberry Pi OS, a network connection, and an address you can reach.

```
git clone https://github.com/glossyio/traffic-monitor
bash traffic-monitor/script/tmsetup.sh -H <address>[,<address>] -l <username> -k -K
```

| Flag | Meaning                                                                           |
| ---- | --------------------------------------------------------------------------------- |
| `-H` | The devices' hostnames or IP addresses, separated by commas                       |
| `-l` | The username you set when imaging the cards. It must be the same on every device. |
| `-k` | Ask for the SSH password                                                          |
| `-K` | Ask for the password for administrator rights. Raspberry Pi OS requires it.       |

Remote devices reboot by themselves when the install needs it. The installer prints a setup code for each device, labeled with the device's address. A remote run doesn't ask for a Wi-Fi country. It keeps the device's, or sets `US` when the device has none; add `-w <code>` to set another, as in [Installer options](https://docs.trafficmonitor.ai/dev/reference/tmsetup/index.md). The hotspot's password isn't printed, because it would end up in the installer's log. Run `sudo tm-control card` on each device to read it.

## Next steps

1. [Choose a site and mount](https://docs.trafficmonitor.ai/dev/deployment-and-mounting-guide/index.md) the device.
1. [First-time setup](https://docs.trafficmonitor.ai/dev/setup-guide/index.md): claim the device, turn on detection, adjust the zones, and record the location.
# Deploy

# Choose a site and mount

Deployment covers where the device goes, how it's mounted, and the angle of the camera and radar to the roadway. The zones and location are set afterwards in [First-time setup](https://docs.trafficmonitor.ai/dev/setup-guide/index.md).

Danger

**Follow the law.** Comply with all applicable laws and local regulations when installing, mounting, and deploying a Traffic Monitor, particularly in public spaces. Unauthorized surveillance can lead to legal consequences and infringe privacy rights. Consult legal professionals or local authorities if you are unsure of the requirements. This guide is for educational purposes; you are responsible for complying with the law and for the consequences of deploying and using the device.

Mount the device only where you have permission, and don't attach it to utility poles without proper authorization.

## Mounting options

Choose a mount that lets you make fine adjustments, because the radar's angle and position need tuning on site.

The open source, 3D-printed [enclosure](https://docs.trafficmonitor.ai/dev/build-your-own-device-diy/recommended-hardware/#enclosure) has several mounting methods built in, depending on the variant:

- 1/4"-20 screw insert on the bottom and back, for camera and trail-camera mounting hardware
- VESA-compatible holes (75 and 100 mm)
- Arca-Swiss-compatible quick-release plate on the bottom, for tripods
- Strap slots on the back, for posts, poles, and trees
- Safety tether hole for a carabiner and strap

Back: VESA holes, 1/4"-20 screw insert, strap slots, and safety tether hole (lower left)

Bottom: Arca-Swiss quick-release plate and 1/4"-20 screw insert

## Temporary deployments

For counts over a few hours, such as an event or a point-in-time study, mount the device at or above head height with an unobstructed view of the roadway. A sturdy tripod and a compact portable power station work well.

On a 16-foot telescoping tripod, counting event participants

Recording manual confirmation counts, with the device on a camera tripod and a portable power station

## Permanent deployments

Warning

**Work safely.** Use proper safety equipment and ladder practice. Make sure the device is securely mounted, all fasteners are tight, the safety tether is in place, and the mount is stable. Failure to do so can cause injury or property damage.

Long-term deployments work anywhere the camera has a good view of the roadway and the radar can be aimed along it: garage roofs, a wood post in a cement-filled bucket, a stone pillar. Keep the device out of reach and clear of anything that might grow or be parked in front of it.

Long-term deployments, with permission, on a private rooftop and a gate entrance

## Best practices

- Mount the device above the roadway and out of reach, about 10 to 12 feet up, for the best view and the least tampering.
- Choose a clear view of the road. Objects are still tracked when they pass briefly behind a tree or lamp post.
- Keep the radar off parking spots and other places where vehicles stop, because stationary vehicles get in the way of its readings.
- The camera detects objects anywhere in its field of view, so frame the whole stretch of road you care about.
- Think about which [zones](https://docs.trafficmonitor.ai/dev/setup-guide/#3-adjust-the-zones) your use case needs, and whether the view lets you draw them.

### Sample deployments

Quiet road, monitoring downhill movement

Busy business district, nearly head-on movement on a wide road

Busy business district, side-on view focused on a pedestrian and bike crosswalk

Neighborhood greenway, an ideal spot to count bikes, pedestrians, and cars

Greenway mounting spot, facing south

Greenway mounting spot, facing north

### Camera considerations

The camera detects objects anywhere in the frame, so cover the whole area of interest even if the roadway isn't centered. An unobstructed view gives the best results.

Detections can happen anywhere in the camera's field of view

### Radar considerations

The radar has a narrower field of view than the camera and measures speed accurately only at a shallow angle to the direction of travel.

- Aim the device so that traffic moves toward or away from it at **45 degrees or less**. The [OmniPreSense field-of-view calculator](https://omnipresense.com/ops243-field-of-view-calculator/) shows how the angle affects the reading.
- The radar labels movement **inbound** (toward the device) and **outbound** (away from it), and the camera uses the same words. Place the device so those directions make sense for your roadway, for example inbound for downhill traffic.
- To find the radar's coverage, have someone hold the radar outside the case and watch the red and blue LEDs on its front as people and vehicles pass. Where the LEDs blink is where to draw `zone_radar`.

## Next steps

Plug the device in. It starts by itself, and the green LED on the Raspberry Pi shows it has power. Continue with [First-time setup](https://docs.trafficmonitor.ai/dev/setup-guide/index.md).

# First-time setup

Do these steps once the device is [mounted](https://docs.trafficmonitor.ai/dev/deployment-and-mounting-guide/index.md) and powered on, and again whenever you move it. You need a computer or phone on the same network or on the device's own hotspot, and the device's setup code or administrator login. A device without a radar also needs an SSH client for step 4.

As installed, the camera and the first radar are turned on in the Traffic Monitor's settings, but Frigate's object detection is off. Nothing is counted until you turn it on in step 2.

## 1. Claim the device

Open `http://<device>/`, where `<device>` is the hostname you set when imaging the card followed by `.local`, or the device's IP address. [Home page and apps](https://docs.trafficmonitor.ai/dev/use/home-page/index.md) explains each link and how to find the address.

A device at the roadside has no network to join. If its Wi-Fi isn't on a network it knows, it runs its own hotspot, named `TM-` and four characters. Join it with the password from the device's card; your phone's sign-in window then opens the setup page by itself, or you can open `http://10.42.0.1/`. [Wi-Fi and the hotspot](https://docs.trafficmonitor.ai/dev/use/wifi-hotspot/index.md) has the details, including what to do on an iPhone or an Android 17 phone.

A device you didn't give a Wi-Fi network when imaging the card is reached through its hotspot. Join it, finish setup below, and then put the device on the network it will use: as the administrator, open **Network**, choose **Refresh**, pick the network, and type its password. The device tests the network and switches to it after a five-minute countdown; [Put the unit on a Wi-Fi network](https://docs.trafficmonitor.ai/dev/use/wifi-hotspot/#put-the-unit-on-a-wi-fi-network) walks through it. A Wi-Fi network you set in Imager works too, and shows up on that page as a saved network.

A device that hasn't been claimed opens its setup page:

1. Choose **Start setup**, and read and accept the license agreement.
1. Enter the setup code from the end of the installer's output, or from the card that came with a pre-built unit. `sudo tm-control card` on the device shows it again.
1. Create the administrator account with a username and password, and choose **Claim this device**.
1. Optionally, set a new system password for Cockpit and SSH.

[Control app and login](https://docs.trafficmonitor.ai/dev/use/control-app/index.md) explains each step, and how to add accounts for other people. If the device was claimed already, log in as the administrator.

## 2. Turn on detection

1. Open **Frigate** from the home page, logged in as the administrator.
1. Go to **Settings > Configuration editor**.
1. Under `cameras: picam_h265: detect:`, change `enabled: false` to `enabled: true`.
1. Choose **Save & Restart**.

When Frigate is back, its live view draws a box around anything that moves past the camera.

## 3. Adjust the zones

The Traffic Monitor looks for four zones with fixed names. Frigate ships with all four drawn for a sample roadway; drag their corners to fit yours.

1. In Frigate, go to **Settings > Camera configuration > Masks / Zones**.
1. Edit each zone in the table below, then save. Frigate restarts.

| Zone           | Draw it over                                                                                                                                            | Used for                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                 |
| -------------- | ------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- | ------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------ |
| `zone_capture` | The whole roadway you want to count, including sidewalks that are clearly in view                                                                       | Counting. An object is counted only if it passes through this zone.                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                      |
| `zone_near`    | The half of `zone_capture` closest to the device                                                                                                        | Direction                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                |
| `zone_far`     | The half of `zone_capture` farthest from the device                                                                                                     | Direction. An object that enters `zone_near` and then `zone_far` is moving **outbound**, away from the device; the reverse is **inbound**.                                                                                                                                                                               |
| `zone_radar`   | The part of the road the radar covers accurately, roughly a rectangle from curb to curb in the middle of the frame. Skip it if the device has no radar. | Speed statistics. Any object that enters a zone gets a speed from the radar, but the dashboards' speed statistics use only objects that passed through this zone. [Radar considerations](https://docs.trafficmonitor.ai/dev/deployment-and-mounting-guide/#radar-considerations) shows how to find the radar's coverage. |

The four zones drawn over a residential street

Zones you draw for your own analysis, such as a stop-sign zone or a crosswalk, can have any other name. [Ideas and use cases](https://docs.trafficmonitor.ai/dev/help-and-faq/use-cases-and-scenarios/index.md) has examples.

## 4. Record the location and sensors

The location is optional. If the device stays in one place and you never share its data, it can count without one. To record where the device is and which way it faces:

1. Open **Location** from the control app's menu, as the administrator.
1. Choose **Add a place**. Enter a description that only you see, paste the latitude and longitude from any maps app, and choose the way each sensor faces. Choose **Save**.
1. Open the new place in the list, choose **Deploy here**, check the review, and choose **Deploy**.

To record only the way the sensors face, choose **Modify deployment** on the place in use, **First location**, and change the bearings there. [Places and location](https://docs.trafficmonitor.ai/dev/use/location/index.md) explains each step, and how precisely the database stores the location.

Then check that the sensors in the Traffic Monitor's settings match the hardware. A device with the Pi camera and one radar needs no change. A device without a radar needs `enabled: false` under `TM_RADAR_SERIAL_PORT_00`. Connect over SSH and open the settings file:

```
sudo nano /opt/traffic-monitor/node-red-tm/config/config.yml
```

The camera and radar, as installed:

```
sensors:
    cameras:
        picam_h265:
            enabled: true
            camera_radar: TM_RADAR_SERIAL_PORT_00
    radars:
        TM_RADAR_SERIAL_PORT_00:
            enabled: true
```

Save with Ctrl+O and leave nano with Ctrl+X. The Traffic Monitor reads the file again as soon as you save it, so no restart is needed. A change that doesn't take effect usually means a YAML error, such as a wrong indent.

[config.yml settings](https://docs.trafficmonitor.ai/dev/configuration/node-red-config/index.md) describes every setting in this file, including the optional [ThingsBoard](https://docs.trafficmonitor.ai/dev/data-and-payloads/integrations/index.md) upload.

## 5. Check the counts

Open **Dashboard** from the home page and choose **Monitoring** in the sidebar. [Monitoring](https://docs.trafficmonitor.ai/dev/ui/monitoring/index.md) shows a count a few seconds after each object passes through `zone_capture`, and speed statistics for objects that also passed through `zone_radar`. Today's counts start at 04:00 local time, so between midnight and 04:00 they're empty.

No counts?

Work down the list:

1. **Frigate shows no boxes around moving objects.** Detection is off (step 2), or the camera is off: in the configuration editor, `cameras: picam_h265:` needs `enabled: true`. If the live view is black, open **Camera feeds** from the home page to check that the camera itself streams.
1. **Frigate detects objects, but the dashboard stays at zero.** The objects aren't passing through `zone_capture` (step 3), or the camera is off in the Traffic Monitor's settings: `sensors: cameras: picam_h265:` needs `enabled: true`, and the name must match Frigate's camera name. If your edits don't take effect, check the file for a YAML error.
1. **Counts but no speeds.** The radar must be `enabled: true` and named in the camera's `camera_radar`, `zone_radar` must cover the road, and the radar must have been plugged in when the software was installed. If you added it later, rerun `bash traffic-monitor/script/tmsetup.sh -t node-red-tm`.
1. **Still nothing.** Look at the logs in [System administration](https://docs.trafficmonitor.ai/dev/use/system-admin/index.md), then ask in the [chat](https://docs.trafficmonitor.ai/dev/help-and-faq/where-can-i-get-support/index.md).
# Use the device

# Control app and login

The device's [home page](https://docs.trafficmonitor.ai/dev/use/home-page/index.md) is its control app. It holds the device's accounts, and one login there opens the apps your account may use: the dashboards, Frigate, the Node-RED editor, and the camera feeds. [Cockpit](https://docs.trafficmonitor.ai/dev/use/system-admin/#cockpit) has its own address and its own login. Its Status, Device, and Date and time pages show whether the device works and help you fix it; see [Check and fix the device](https://docs.trafficmonitor.ai/dev/use/device-health/index.md). Its Detection page shows the object detection model and lets the administrator change it; see [Choose the detection model](https://docs.trafficmonitor.ai/dev/use/detection/index.md). Its Location page records where the device is and how precisely the database stores it; see [Places and location](https://docs.trafficmonitor.ai/dev/use/location/index.md). These accounts belong to the device. They're separate from the Raspberry Pi user account you created when you imaged the card. That account's password is the **system password**.

What the login protects

The login keeps people on your network out of the apps. The device uses plain HTTP, so passwords and images cross your network unencrypted. Use the device on a network you trust.

## Claim the device

A device that has no administrator yet sends every page to setup. That happens on a new device, after an update from a version without the login, and after [`reset-admin`](#if-the-administrators-password-is-lost). Setup has four steps: a welcome page, the license agreement, the administrator account, and the system password.

You need the **setup code**, eight letters and digits written as `XXXX-XXXX`. It comes from one of two places:

- **A pre-built unit:** the card that came with the device.

- **A device you installed yourself:** the end of the installer's output, in a line like this one:

  ```
  This device isn't claimed yet. Open http://tm-01.local/ (or its IP address) and enter the setup code ABCD-EFGH
  to create the administrator account. The code works once.
  ```

  The installer prints the same code on every run until the device is claimed. The installer's log, `~/tmsetup-<date>-<time>.log` on the computer that ran it, has the same output. On the device, `sudo tm-control card` shows the code with the device's hotspot name and password, and `sudo cat /etc/traffic-monitor/setup-code` shows the code alone.

To claim the device:

1. Open `http://<device>/`. [Home page and apps](https://docs.trafficmonitor.ai/dev/use/home-page/index.md) explains how to find the address. On the device's own hotspot, the phone's sign-in window opens it for you; see [Wi-Fi and the hotspot](https://docs.trafficmonitor.ai/dev/use/wifi-hotspot/index.md).
1. Choose **Start setup**, read the license agreement, and accept it.
1. Enter the setup code, then a username and password for the administrator account. Usernames are 3 to 32 characters: lowercase letters, digits, dots, dashes, and underscores. Passwords are at least 10 characters.
1. Choose **Claim this device**. You're logged in as the administrator.
1. Set a new [system password](#the-system-password), or choose **Skip for now**.

Step 3 of setup creates the administrator account

The code works once. After several wrong codes, setup makes you wait before the next try, a little longer after each wrong code.

When the license agreement changes

An update can bring a new version of the license agreement. Until the administrator accepts it, nobody can open the apps. The administrator sees the new version after logging in. Viewers see **Waiting for an administrator** until it's accepted.

## The system password

The system password is the password of the Raspberry Pi user account: the one you log in to Cockpit and SSH with. Setup offers to change it, with a **Use the same password as my account** checkbox. Skip the step to keep the password the account has. To change it later, use Cockpit's **Accounts** page, or run `passwd` over SSH.

If someone else installed the device, you may not know the account's name. Setup's system-password step and the home page's **Cockpit** tile show it to the administrator.

## Log in

Open the home page or any app. Without a session, the device shows its login page, then takes you to the page you asked for. You stay logged in for a week, and using the device keeps the session going. To log out, choose **Log out** in the menu. Frigate's own **Logout** also logs you out of the device.

After five wrong passwords in a row, the device makes you wait before the next try: a few seconds at first, and twice as long after each further wrong password, up to 5 minutes. It counts wrong passwords for the account and for the address they come from, so a wait for an account applies on every phone and computer. Sessions that are already logged in keep working. The count clears 15 minutes after the last wrong password, or when the login succeeds.

## Administrators and viewers

Each device has one administrator, the account created when it was claimed, and any number of viewers.

| App or page                                                                                  | Administrator | Viewer                                                                                                    |
| -------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- | ------------- | --------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- |
| Dashboard and Legacy Dashboard                                                               | Yes           | Yes                                                                                                       |
| Downloads on the [Data export](https://docs.trafficmonitor.ai/dev/ui/database/index.md) page | Yes           | No                                                                                                        |
| Frigate: live view, review, and explore                                                      | Yes           | Yes                                                                                                       |
| Frigate: settings and the configuration editor                                               | Yes           | No                                                                                                        |
| Node-RED editor and Camera feeds                                                             | Yes           | No                                                                                                        |
| The **Users** page                                                                           | Yes           | No                                                                                                        |
| Status, Device, and Date and time pages                                                      | Yes           | Read only; see [What viewers see](https://docs.trafficmonitor.ai/dev/use/device-health/#what-viewers-see) |
| The **Detection** page                                                                       | Yes           | Read only; see [The Detection page](https://docs.trafficmonitor.ai/dev/use/detection/#the-detection-page) |
| The **Location** page                                                                        | Yes           | No                                                                                                        |

Cockpit uses the Raspberry Pi user account, not these accounts.

### Add a viewer

1. Open **Users** from the menu.
1. Under **Add a viewer**, enter a username and a password, and choose **Add viewer**.
1. Give the person the username and password.

Each viewer's menu on the **Users** page has **Set a new password**, which also logs them out everywhere, and **Remove**.

## Change your password

Open **Account** from the menu. Under **Change your password**, enter your current password and the new one. Every other browser and phone where you were logged in is logged out; this one stays logged in. Wrong current passwords count toward the same wait as wrong logins.

**Log out everywhere**, on the same page, ends your sessions in every browser and on every phone, including the one you're using. Use it if you logged in on a device that isn't yours.

## If you forget a password

- **A viewer's password:** the administrator sets a new one on the **Users** page.
- **The administrator's password:** see the next section.

### If the administrator's password is lost

Someone who can log in to the device with the Raspberry Pi user account can start over. Open a terminal over SSH, or in Cockpit at `http://<device>:9090`, and run:

```
sudo tm-control reset-admin
```

It removes every account, the administrator and all viewers, and prints a new setup code. Then [claim the device](#claim-the-device) again with that code. Your data and settings stay as they are.

## If the control app is down

When the control app doesn't answer, the apps can't check your login. Every app then shows a page that says the control app isn't answering, and the home page says **The control app isn't answering**. To start it again:

- In a browser, open Cockpit at `http://<device>:9090`. It doesn't need the control app. Log in with your Raspberry Pi user account, go to **Services**, open `tm-control.service`, and restart it.

- Over SSH, run:

  ```
  sudo systemctl restart tm-control.service
  sudo journalctl -u tm-control.service -n 50   # if it stops again, the reason is in its log
  ```

An app that's down while the control app works, such as Frigate during a restart, shows a `502 Bad Gateway` error instead. [System administration](https://docs.trafficmonitor.ai/dev/use/system-admin/index.md) covers the services and their logs.

# Choose the detection model

The control app's **Detection** page shows what the device looks for and which AI model does the looking, and lets the administrator change the model without SSH. [Frigate](https://docs.trafficmonitor.ai/dev/configuration/frigate-config/index.md) runs the model on the device's detector: a Coral or Hailo accelerator, or the processor when there's none. To get a better model for a difficult site, see [Better models](https://docs.trafficmonitor.ai/dev/configuration/frigate-config/#better-models).

## The Detection page

**Detection** is in the control app's menu, after **Device**. The page opens with a line on what it's for, then four sections:

- **Object detection** gives the **Detector**, such as `edgetpu` for a Coral, and the **Running model**, then [what the running model recognises](#what-the-model-recognises) and what the device tracks.
- **Model in use** is the model Frigate runs. The section is left out when the page can't tell which model that is.
- **Other models on this device** lists the rest, and its title counts them.
- **[Frigate+](#frigate-plus)** is how to get a Frigate+ model, and where administrators set the API key.

Each model is a card with its name, its kind (Frigate+ or local), and when it was trained and what it's built for (when it says). Select **Files and objects** on a card to see its files, with their sizes and the start of each file's SHA-256 hash, and [the objects it recognises](#what-the-model-recognises). A model with no list of objects has **Files** instead. A mark says when the model is:

| Mark                       | Meaning                                                                       |
| -------------------------- | ----------------------------------------------------------------------------- |
| In use                     | Frigate runs this model.                                                      |
| can't run on this detector | The model is built for another detector than the device's, so **Use** is off. |
| incomplete                 | The model has its file but not its `.json`, or the other way round.           |

The model the installer set up is shown as **The installer's model**. It has no `.json`, and it can't be deleted. A device without a Coral has no installer's model: Frigate then runs its own built-in model until you choose another, and the page shows it as **Frigate's built-in model**, which can't be deleted either.

Everyone who can log in sees the models, the label lists, and the Frigate+ text. Administrators also get **Upload a model**, under the **Other models on this device** heading, then **Use**, **Download**, and **Delete** on each model, and the Frigate+ API key. While Frigate runs another model, the device's default (the installer's model, or Frigate's built-in model on a device without a Coral) has a **Use** of its own.

When Frigate isn't answering, the page says so and shows what Frigate's config file says. The same when Frigate started in safe mode because it couldn't use its config: the page says so, nothing is detected meanwhile, and **Use** on a model, or on the installer's model, gives Frigate a config it can run.

## Upload a model

A model is a model file and a small `.json` file beside it, its *sidecar*, which tells Frigate how to use it. Choose **Upload a model** under **Other models on this device**, then pick one of these:

- **A package** from whoever trained the model: a zip or tar.gz with the model file and its `.json` at the top level, not inside a folder. A zip must be stored or deflate-compressed, which is what ordinary zip tools make. If the package has a `SHA256SUMS` file, the device checks the files against it.
- **The two files**, the model file and its `.json`. The `.json` must be named for the model file: `mine.tflite` and `mine.tflite.json`. The page sends the `.json` first.
- **A model file alone.** The page then asks for what Frigate needs to know about it and writes the `.json` for you. The settings are a name for the model list (the file name when left empty), the model type, the width and height of its input, the input tensor, the pixel format, optionally the input data type, and the labels, one per line in the model's order. On a device with a Coral or Hailo accelerator, the fields start with Frigate's example for that detector. The values come from the model's documentation; Frigate's [reference config](https://docs.frigate.video/configuration/advanced/reference) lists what each setting accepts.
- **A `.json` alone**, to finish a model file that's on the device already.

The page shows every file when you pick, because a Frigate+ model's file has no extension.

The limits are 100 MB for a model file, 2 MB for a `.json`, and at least 512 MB of free storage left afterwards. A model whose name is already on the device is refused; delete the old one first. A model file can't be named `default`, which the page keeps for the device's default. A model has to be built for the device's detector. The page marks one that isn't, and won't use it.

Take models only from a source you trust

A model is code that the detector runs. A model from an unknown source can make the device count wrongly or fail. Upload only models you trained, or that come from a source you trust.

## Use a model

Choose **Use** on a model and confirm. Frigate checks the whole configuration with the model in it and saves it, and then the device restarts Frigate. A restart takes about a minute, and the device counts nothing meanwhile. The page asks every few seconds and says when Frigate runs the model. If Frigate hasn't come back after 90 seconds, the page says so and links to the [Status page](https://docs.trafficmonitor.ai/dev/use/device-health/#the-status-page).

If Frigate refuses the change, the page shows Frigate's reason, and nothing changes. When Frigate isn't answering at all, the device edits Frigate's `config.yml` itself, keeps a backup beside it, and restarts Frigate. That's how **Use** on **The installer's model** gets a device out of a bad choice without SSH. On a device without a Coral, **Use** on **Frigate's built-in model** does the same.

The page refuses a **Use** in these cases:

- Frigate is restarting. Try again in a minute.
- The device's detector can't be told, because Frigate isn't answering and its config file can't be read, so the model can't be checked against it.
- Frigate's config sets a model inside a detector, which would override this one. Remove that model in Frigate's config editor first.
- The installer's model file is gone from the device.

## Download a model

**Download** saves a zip with the model's file, its `.json`, and a `SHA256SUMS` file. The files are byte for byte what's on the device, so the zip is a backup, or a way to put the same model on another device with **Upload a model**. A `.json` keeps every field it came with, including ones the page doesn't show.

A model without a `.json` the device can read downloads as its model file alone, under the file's own name, and the page says so before it starts. Whoever uploads that file is asked for [what Frigate needs to know about it](#upload-a-model). The installer's model and Frigate's built-in model download this way too. A device keeps their file names for its own copies, so rename such a file before you upload it.

## Delete a model

**Delete** asks first, then removes both of the model's files. It can't remove the model Frigate runs, the installer's model, or Frigate's built-in model. To delete the model that's running, use another model first, such as **The installer's model**.

## What the model recognises

The **Object detection** section lists two sets of objects. Each is closed until you select its title, which counts the objects, and each has a **Copy** button:

- **Objects the running model recognises** is what the running model can detect. The list says where it came from: Frigate when it answers, otherwise the model's `.json` or the installer's labels file. Objects the device also tracks are filled. Frigate fills the gaps in a model's label map with entries named `unknown`, which the page leaves out, so its count can be lower than the label map's.
- **Objects tracked on this device** is the objects Frigate is set to track, from its `objects:` `track` lists. Objects the running model doesn't recognise are amber, and the title counts them.

Frigate tracks only the objects in both lists. To track more of what the model recognises, change the lists in Frigate's configuration editor; see [Tune object detection](https://docs.trafficmonitor.ai/dev/configuration/frigate-config/index.md). An object that's tracked but not recognised is also named under the two lists, so you see it while they're closed. The model can't detect it, so the device never counts it.

Each model's card has its own list under **Files and objects**, read from that model's `.json` or, for the installer's model, its labels file. Frigate's built-in model has none. On the other models' cards, a line names the tracked objects that model doesn't recognise, which the device would stop counting if you switched to it.

The running model's list and its card are read in different ways, but they should agree. When Frigate's list has different objects, a line under the facts says "Frigate reports a different list than this model's .json." This is rare, and it usually means someone edited the label map in Frigate's config on purpose.

## Frigate+

[Frigate+](https://docs.trafficmonitor.ai/dev/configuration/frigate-config/#better-models) trains models on snapshots from your device. There are two ways to get one onto it:

- **Online:** when the device has internet and a Frigate+ API key, pick the model in Frigate, under **Settings > System > Detectors and model**, and Frigate downloads it. Then choose [Use](#use-a-model) here if Frigate doesn't run it already.
- **Offline:** upload the model's two files on this page, as a package from whoever trained the model, or copied from another device's Frigate. See [A device without internet](https://docs.trafficmonitor.ai/dev/configuration/frigate-config/#a-device-without-internet).

Administrators enter the API key under **Frigate+**, the last section of the page, which is closed until you select its title. The Status page's **Set the key** opens it. The key is kept with the device's other secrets, not in `config.yml`.

- The page never shows the key back. The section's title says whether the key is set, its last four characters for a key of 12 or more characters, and "in use" while Frigate runs a Frigate+ model.
- **Save** stores what you typed. A key is 36 characters, a colon, and 40 lowercase letters or digits, as Frigate+ shows it; the page refuses anything else. The eye icon shows the key while you type.
- **Remove** asks first, then empties the key. Without a key, snapshots can't be submitted to Frigate+. A Frigate+ model whose files are on the device keeps running; one that isn't downloaded yet [stops Frigate](https://docs.trafficmonitor.ai/dev/configuration/frigate-config/#if-frigate-stops-over-a-model) until the key is set again, and the Status page's Frigate+ check says so.
- Saving or removing restarts Frigate, which takes about a minute. The device counts nothing meanwhile.

The ThingsBoard and Plate Recognizer keys are on the [Device page](https://docs.trafficmonitor.ai/dev/use/device-health/#tokens-and-keys).

# Check and fix the device

Four pages in the [control app](https://docs.trafficmonitor.ai/dev/use/control-app/index.md)'s menu tell you whether the device works and let the administrator fix the common problems from a phone, without SSH. A fifth, [Detection](https://docs.trafficmonitor.ai/dev/use/detection/index.md), shows the object detection model and changes it:

- **Status** checks the services, apps, settings, hardware, network, and clock, and offers a fix for what's wrong.
- **Device** shows the device's facts and software versions, and has the diagnostics download, reboot, and shut down.
- **Date and time** compares the device's clock with your phone's or computer's and sets it.
- **Network** shows the device's names and addresses, and lets the administrator change the hotspot. See [The Network page](https://docs.trafficmonitor.ai/dev/use/wifi-hotspot/#the-network-page).

The [home page](https://docs.trafficmonitor.ai/dev/use/home-page/index.md) shows the Status page's summary under the device's name, such as **Everything is working**. Tap it to open the Status page.

## The Status page

The page opens with one sentence about the whole device:

| Summary                           | Meaning                                                                    |
| --------------------------------- | -------------------------------------------------------------------------- |
| Everything is working             | Every check passed.                                                        |
| Working, with 2 things to look at | Some checks have a warning, and none has a problem.                        |
| 2 problems need attention         | At least one check has a problem.                                          |
| Some checks couldn't run          | Some checks couldn't get an answer, and none found a warning or a problem. |

Below it, each check shows a mark, its name, and one or two sentences about what it found and what to do. A tick means it passed, a triangle a warning, a cross a problem, and a question mark that the check couldn't run. The page checks again every 10 seconds while it's open. **Refresh** checks at once.

The checks come in groups:

| Group         | What it checks                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                |
