The warning says: "With the hotspot off, this unit has no wireless way in when its Wi-Fi network is missing. You would need an Ethernet cable." The hotspot stops now and doesn't start by itself again, and phones on it are disconnected. To turn it on again, switch **Hotspot on** back on. The unit then starts the hotspot as the table above describes; a unit that is on a saved network starts it when that network is lost.

## The password

The installer makes the password on the unit, at random, when it sets up the hotspot. It's twelve letters and digits in three groups, such as `ABCD-EFGH-JKLM`, and it's different on every unit. It never comes from the serial number, so knowing the name tells nobody the password.

The unit keeps it in `/etc/traffic-monitor/secrets/hotspot_password`, readable only by root and the installing user's group (`tmadmin` unless you installed with `-g`). The installer shows the card on the terminal and keeps the password out of its log; a run from another computer with `-H` prints only a reminder of the command.

### Show the password

On the Network page, an administrator opens **Hotspot** and chooses **Show** next to **Password**. The page asks the unit for the password each time and forgets it again when you choose **Hide**, change anything, or leave the page. The control app records each time an administrator shows it.

If you can't sign in, run `sudo tm-control card` on the unit instead. Over Ethernet or SSH works when you're locked out of the hotspot.

### Change the password

1. Sign in as an administrator and open **Network**, then open **Hotspot**.
1. Next to **Password**, choose **Change**. A unit whose hotspot has no password offers **Set a password** here.
1. Type the new password, 8 to 63 letters, digits, and symbols with no space at either end.
1. Write the password down, then choose **Change password**, or **Set password** on a unit that has none.

The hotspot restarts with the new password, and phones on it are disconnected. Each phone must rejoin by hand, with the new password. The page types the password in the open and asks for it only once, so you see what you write down.

### For sellers

`sudo tm-control card --json` prints the card's values as JSON, for a label or a packing slip:

```
{
  "hostname": "tm-01",
  "local_url": "http://tm-01.local/",
  "hotspot": {"name": "TM-4F2A", "password": "ABCD-EFGH-JKLM", "url": "http://10.42.0.1/"},
  "claimed": false,
  "setup_code": "ABCD-EFGH"
}
```

`setup_code` is `null` once the unit is claimed. The command needs `sudo`, and it prints to the terminal only. Nothing stores or logs the card, so don't paste the output where others can read it.

## Rename the hotspot or hide its name

An administrator can change the name phones see, and hide it, in the **Hotspot** panel of the Network page.

### Rename the hotspot

1. Open **Network**, open **Hotspot**, and next to its **Name**, choose **Change**.
1. Type the new name. It takes 1 to 32 bytes, so fewer characters if it has accents or emoji, with no space at either end.
1. Choose **Change name**.

The hotspot restarts, and each phone must join the new name by hand. A printed card still shows the old name. `sudo tm-control card` shows the new one.

### Hide the name

1. Open **Network**, open **Hotspot**, and switch on **Hide the name**.
1. Read the warning, and choose **Hide the name**.

The warning says: "The hotspot is still on and can still be found by scanning. Only its name is hidden." Hiding the name doesn't stop anyone from finding the hotspot, so it isn't a lock. A phone no longer lists the hotspot by name. On Android, add the network by hand: choose **Add network**, type the name and the password, and tick **Hidden network**. Without that, the phone never connects. Switch **Hide the name** off to show the name again.

## A hotspot you set up by hand

A hotspot you made yourself in NetworkManager is kept. When a unit has no profile named `tm-hotspot`, the installer takes over your access-point profile, the one that starts by itself and was used last, renames it `tm-hotspot`, and stops any other access point from starting. Its name on air, password, band, and hidden setting stay as you set them. The installer sets the profile's address to `10.42.0.1` and its priority below your saved networks, and copies the password into the password file.

A hand-made hotspot with no password shows as a problem on the Status page, because anyone nearby can join it. The Status page's **Set a password** link opens the Network page with **Hotspot** open. There, next to **Password**, choose **Set a password** and follow the steps in [Change the password](#change-the-password). The installer then keeps the profile's password the same as the password file's. An empty file tells the installer to leave the hotspot's security alone.

A hand-made hotspot with a hidden name keeps it. Manage it as in [Hide the name](#hide-the-name).

## Who can see the hotspot

A hotspot on a pole is visible to anyone passing, and public Wi-Fi maps record where names are seen. The name `TM-` and four characters shows that a Traffic Monitor is nearby and doesn't say where it is. [Hiding the name](#hide-the-name) makes the hotspot harder to spot in a list, but a scan still finds it. Only turning the hotspot off prevents it, with the cost described in [Turn the hotspot off](#turn-the-hotspot-off). The password is what keeps people out of the control app. [Control app and login](https://docs.trafficmonitor.ai/dev/use/control-app/index.md) explains what its login protects.

## The Wi-Fi country

Wi-Fi rules differ by country, and a radio with no country set uses limited worldwide settings. The installer asks for the country, as a two-letter code such as `US` or `GB`, when the unit has none. Press Enter to accept `US`. With `-y`, it keeps the unit's country, or sets `US` when there is none. To set it without being asked, or to change it, run the installer with `-w`:

```
bash traffic-monitor/script/tmsetup.sh -t wifi -w GB
```

The change applies at once, with no reboot. The Status page warns while no country is set.

## Limits

- The page can't join an open network, a hidden network (a saved hidden network included), a WPA3-only network, or a network that asks for a user name as well as a password (an enterprise network). It lists open, WPA3-only, enterprise, and other kinds with the reason, such as "Open networks can't be joined." or "This kind of network can't be joined." A hidden network is never listed by a scan, and a saved hidden network shows a **Hidden** mark and has no **Join**. A network that offers both WPA2 and WPA3 is joined as WPA2. The page doesn't complete a sign-in page, it only reports one.
- One join (the test, the countdown, and the switch) runs at a time, and the page joins over IPv4 only.
- A network the unit is also connected to that uses `10.42.0.x` addresses clashes with the hotspot's fixed address. Give that network another range.
- The hotspot runs on the built-in radio, `wlan0`. If a USB Wi-Fi adapter takes that name, the hotspot stays off, and the Status page says so. Unplug the adapter and reboot.

______________________________________________________________________

## description: The Data export dashboard: download the database or a JSON export, and add comments for whoever analyzes the data.

# Data export

Open `http://<device>/dashboard/database`, or **Database** in the dashboard's sidebar. This page gets data off the device and lets you leave notes in it. Both downloads need the device's administrator login; a [viewer](https://docs.trafficmonitor.ai/dev/use/control-app/#administrators-and-viewers) can open the page but not download.

The Data export page

## Comments

A comment is a timestamped note stored in the `comments` table, for whoever analyzes the data later: a settings change, road work, an event in the area. Give it an effective date and an optional expiry date, the text, and your name; only the name is required. The form also has time fields, but only the dates are kept. Without an effective date, the comment takes effect when you save it. [Data and privacy](https://docs.trafficmonitor.ai/dev/data-and-payloads/data-overview/#comments) lists the columns.

## Download the database

Downloads the whole database as a compressed archive named `<hostname>_<time>_tmdb.tar.gz`. The page shows the database's size in megabytes. The device first makes a consistent copy of the database, so a large one can take a minute or two before the download starts. The copy needs free space about the size of the database; if there isn't enough, the page says so. A 3 GB file can then take about 5 minutes to compress and several more to download. Cancel also works while the copy is being made: the download stops once the copy is done, and no archive is sent. If a download fails, you see the reason instead of a broken file.

On a phone joined to the unit's hotspot, see [Phones](https://docs.trafficmonitor.ai/dev/use/wifi-hotspot/#phones) for how downloads save on Android and on an iPhone.

Unpack the archive with `tar -xvzf` on Linux or Mac, or with [7-Zip](https://www.7-zip.org/) on Windows. Inside is `tmdb.sqlite`, which opens in [DB Browser for SQLite](https://sqlitebrowser.org/) or any SQLite library.

## Download JSON

Exports part of the data as JSON files in a compressed archive named `<hostname>_<time>_json.tar.gz`. Choose what to export and a start and end time, which default to the last 7 days:

| Choice                                     | Contents                                                              |
| ------------------------------------------ | --------------------------------------------------------------------- |
| Everything                                 | The `events` table, the five radar tables, and the `airquality` table |
| All event types                            | The whole `events` table for the time range                           |
| One object type, such as `car` or `person` | The events of that type                                               |
| Air quality                                | The `airquality` table                                                |
| Radar                                      | The radar tables                                                      |

The files are plain JSON, readable in any text editor or loaded straight into a notebook.

______________________________________________________________________

## description: The Monitoring dashboard: today's counts, car speed statistics, hourly and daily charts, and the latest events with their radar readings.

# Monitoring

Open `http://<device>/dashboard/monitoring`, or open **Dashboard** from the home page and choose **Monitoring** in the sidebar. Monitoring shows the counts and speed statistics for one camera and one radar at a time.

The Monitoring page, numbered as in the list below

1. **Sensor selection.** A radar and a camera picker, listing every sensor in [config.yml](https://docs.trafficmonitor.ai/dev/configuration/node-red-config/#sensorscameras), enabled or not. The counts and statistics on this page follow the camera and radar selected on the legacy dashboard at `http://<device>/ui/`, not the selection here. On a device with one camera and one radar, they're the same.

1. **Car speed statistics** for the current day, which starts at 04:00 local time. They cover `car` events that passed through both `zone_capture` and `zone_radar` and got a speed from the radar. Speeds are absolute values, so inbound and outbound are pooled, and every value is rounded to a whole number.

   The percentiles come from sorting the day's cars by speed and splitting them into 20 groups of equal size, so they're approximate. With few cars, some stay empty: the 25th percentile needs 5 cars, the median 10, the 75th percentile and `iqr_upper` 15, and the 85th percentile 17.

   | Statistic                                          | Meaning                                                                                                                                                     |
   | -------------------------------------------------- | ----------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- |
   | `count`                                            | Cars with a speed                                                                                                                                           |
   | `mean_speed`                                       | Average speed                                                                                                                                               |
   | `p25_speed`, `p50_speed`, `p75_speed`, `p85_speed` | 25th, 50th (median), 75th, and 85th [percentile](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Percentile) speeds. The 85th percentile is the usual basis for speed limits. |
   | `max_speed`                                        | Fastest car                                                                                                                                                 |
   | `count_over_25`                                    | Cars faster than 25, in the radar's units                                                                                                                   |
   | `iqr_upper`                                        | The outlier line: `p75_speed` plus 1.5 times the [interquartile range](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Interquartile_range)                                   |
   | `iqr_upper_freq`                                   | Cars faster than `iqr_upper`, the outliers                                                                                                                  |

1. **Today's counts** by object type for events that passed through `zone_capture`. The day starts at 04:00 local time, so from midnight until 04:00 these counts and the speed statistics are empty. Objects that pass in those hours are left out of the day's counts, but they appear in the hourly and daily charts.

1. **Hourly counts** by object type for the last 36 hours, for events that passed through `zone_capture`.

1. **Daily counts** by object type for the last 10 calendar days, for events that passed through `zone_capture`.

1. **Latest observations.** The 21 most recent events from any camera that passed through `zone_radar`, newest first, including events without a speed. Each card shows Frigate's thumbnail of the object, the direction, the speed, and the radar's raw readings from the start of the event to its end: how many there were ("radar hits"), the range of their magnitudes and speeds, and two charts, **Radar Magnitude** and **Radar Speed**. The charts show whether the readings came from one object or from several at once. They're the raw readings, not the ones the speed was worked out from. The list is kept in memory, so it empties when Node-RED restarts.

Counts and statistics come from the `events` table; see [Events](https://docs.trafficmonitor.ai/dev/data-and-payloads/events-payload/index.md). The same counts are published over MQTT on `tm/events`; see [MQTT and ThingsBoard](https://docs.trafficmonitor.ai/dev/data-and-payloads/integrations/#tmevents).

______________________________________________________________________

## description: The Movements dashboard: counts of objects by the sequence of zones they passed through, for checking against manual counts.

# Movements

Open `http://<device>/dashboard/movements`. Movements counts objects by the path they took through your zones, which is how you check the device against a manual count or confirm that the zones capture what you want.

Movements come from the `entered_zones` of each [event](https://docs.trafficmonitor.ai/dev/data-and-payloads/events-payload/index.md), so they depend on how the [zones](https://docs.trafficmonitor.ai/dev/setup-guide/#3-adjust-the-zones) are drawn.

The Movements page

1. **Zones.** Tick the zones to include. The four standard `zone_*` zones are unticked by default, so that zones you drew for your own analysis stand out.
1. **Intermediate zones.** Choose **Show intermediate zones** to count each full sequence of zones separately, or **Show just initial & final zones** to group by where an object entered and where it left.
1. **Time range.** Start and end times; the last 7 days by default. In time zones east of UTC, or with a half-hour offset, the page shows no counts for any range.
1. **Counts** by object type for each zone sequence that matches.

## Example: a complex intersection

An intersection with many zones has dozens of possible movements. Each turn or crossing becomes its own row, which you can compare with a manual count sheet.

Twelve zones drawn on a busy five-way intersection

Manual confirmation counts; the left sheet matches the zones above

# Tune object detection

[Frigate](https://frigate.video/) does the object detection. How well it works depends on the mounting height and angle, the camera, and the weather, so expect to adjust it for each site. The Traffic Monitor is not affiliated with the Frigate project.

The Traffic Monitor's [default Frigate config](https://github.com/glossyio/traffic-monitor/blob/main/container/frigate/config/config.yml.j2) is tuned for roadways seen from an oblique angle, with a side view of objects as they pass. Everything in it can be changed in Frigate's own UI, at **Settings > Configuration editor**, when you're logged in to the device as the administrator. Frigate's [configuration reference](https://docs.frigate.video/configuration/) explains every setting.

Frigate's own login is off. The device's [login](https://docs.trafficmonitor.ai/dev/use/control-app/index.md) passes your username and role on to Frigate: the administrator gets Frigate's admin role, and viewers its viewer role, which can watch and review but not change settings. Frigate's **Logout** logs you out of the device. Keep `auth: enabled: false` and the `proxy:` section as they are; with Frigate's login on, Frigate asks for a second login of its own, separate from the device's accounts.

## See what Frigate sees

Go to **Settings > Debug** to watch detections live with their scores, and the motion regions Frigate is checking. **Explore** lists past detections with their snapshots, which is the quickest way to find missed bikes or a tree that's being called a person.

The debug view shows how detection is performing

## Object filters

Frigate tracks `bicycle`, `person`, `car`, `bus`, `motorcycle`, and `dog` by default. Each object type has two scores in the `objects: filters:` section of the config:

- `min_score` is the score needed to start tracking an object.
- `threshold` is the average score an object needs, over the time it's tracked, to count as a real detection.

The defaults set `bicycle` low, so most kinds of bike are detected, and `motorcycle` high, so a large e-bike isn't called a motorcycle. If you see false positives for a type, raise its `threshold`; if you miss objects, lower it. Frigate's [object filters](https://docs.frigate.video/configuration/object_filters/#object-scores) page describes these and the size and shape filters.

## Masks

Go to **Settings > Camera configuration > Masks / Zones**.

- A **motion mask** stops motion in an area, such as swaying branches or a timestamp overlay, from triggering detection.
- An **object mask** ignores detections of one object type in an area, such as a parked car that's detected every time the light changes.

Warning

Use masks sparingly. Over-masking makes objects harder to track. A motion mask isn't the tool for cutting false positives; adjust the object filters first.

Frigate's [masks](https://docs.frigate.video/configuration/masks) page has the details.

## Higher-resolution stream

The Pi camera is set up to produce two streams. Frigate uses `picam_h265_detect` at 1536×864 by default, which gives the best balance of detail and load. A second stream, `picam_h265_detect_hr`, runs at 2304×1296 for cases where objects are small in the frame.

To switch, change two things in the configuration editor under `cameras: picam_h265:`: the input `path` to `rtsp://{FRIGATE_GO2RTC_RTSP_USER}:{FRIGATE_GO2RTC_RTSP_PASSWORD}@host.containers.internal:8554/picam_h265_detect_hr`, and `detect: width: 2304` with `height: 1296`. Frigate fills in the `{…}` values from `frigate.env`. Then redraw the [zones](https://docs.trafficmonitor.ai/dev/setup-guide/#3-adjust-the-zones) for the new frame size. The higher resolution costs CPU and may lower the frame rate on a busy road.

## Recordings and snapshots

By default, Frigate keeps a cropped snapshot of each detection and a recording of each alert and detection for about an hour, so you can check what was detected. The `record:` and `snapshots:` sections control this: set `enabled: false` to keep nothing, or raise `retain: days` to keep more. [Data and privacy](https://docs.trafficmonitor.ai/dev/data-and-payloads/data-overview/index.md) describes what the device stores.

Frigate can also publish a cropped snapshot of each detected object on the device's [MQTT broker](https://docs.trafficmonitor.ai/dev/data-and-payloads/integrations/#mqtt). The Traffic Monitor doesn't use these snapshots, so new installs turn them off with `mqtt: enabled: false` under `cameras: picam_h265:`. On an older install, add those lines in the configuration editor. Frigate keeps publishing the events the Traffic Monitor counts.

```
cameras:
  picam_h265:
    mqtt:
      enabled: false
```

## Better models

[Frigate+](https://docs.frigate.video/plus/) is a paid service from the Frigate project, separate from the Traffic Monitor. You submit snapshots from your device, label them on the Frigate+ website, and Frigate+ trains a model on them, which can raise accuracy for a difficult site. Its documentation covers the account, labeling, and training.

### Enter the key

Frigate+ gives your account an API key. Enter it on the control app's Detection page, under [Frigate+](https://docs.trafficmonitor.ai/dev/use/detection/#frigate-plus). The page checks the key's format, so a mis-pasted key is caught there. Saving or removing the key restarts Frigate, which takes about a minute. Traffic isn't counted until it's back.

### Submit snapshots

The key is all Frigate needs to submit snapshots. Open **Explore** in Frigate, select a detection, and submit its snapshot to Frigate+. The default config keeps snapshots on, but only for about an hour (see [Recordings and snapshots](#recordings-and-snapshots)), so submit them soon or keep them longer.

A snapshot you submit leaves the device: Frigate sends it to Frigate+, and it can show people.

### Use a model

A model trained by Frigate+ has to be built for the device's detector:

| Device            | Detector type to choose in Frigate+ |
| ----------------- | ----------------------------------- |
| Coral accelerator | `edgetpu`                           |
| Hailo accelerator | `hailo8l`                           |
| No accelerator    | `cpu`                               |

Choose the `yolov9` model type; `mobiledet` is the older one. The [Status page](https://docs.trafficmonitor.ai/dev/use/device-health/#the-status-page) tells you which detector the device has, in its Hardware group.

To use a model on a device that's online, either:

- pick it in Frigate's **Settings > System > Detectors and model**, or

- in **Settings > Configuration editor**, replace the whole `model:` section with only the model's path, then choose **Save & Restart**:

  ```
  model:
    path: plus://<model id>
  ```

  Remove every other key under `model:`; Frigate+ supplies them.

Frigate checks a model before it saves the change: if the model isn't on the device yet, it fetches it with your key, and if the key is missing or wrong, the model id is wrong, or the device is offline, it refuses the change, shows why, and changes nothing. A model it accepts is on the device as two files in `/opt/traffic-monitor/frigate/config/model_cache/`, named after the model id: `<model id>` and `<model id>.json`. Frigate loads it when it restarts.

### A device without internet

Frigate downloads a model only when one of its two files is missing, so a device that's offline can use a Frigate+ model too:

1. On another computer, download the model from Frigate+. You get two files: `<model id>` and `<model id>.json`.
1. On the control app's [Detection page](https://docs.trafficmonitor.ai/dev/use/detection/#upload-a-model), choose **Upload a model** and pick both files. You can also upload a package from whoever trained the model, or the two files from another device, which you can [download](https://docs.trafficmonitor.ai/dev/use/detection/#download-a-model) from its Detection page.
1. Choose **Use** on the model. Frigate reads the two files when it checks the config, without contacting Frigate+, and the device restarts Frigate. If either file is missing, Frigate refuses the change, because it would have to download the model.

The key is then needed only to submit snapshots, which takes internet as well.

### A model of your own

You can also run a model that doesn't come from Frigate+. On the [Detection page](https://docs.trafficmonitor.ai/dev/use/detection/#upload-a-model), upload the model's file with its `.json`, or upload the file alone and fill in what Frigate needs to know about it; the page writes the `.json`. Choose **Use**, and the page writes the model's `model:` section for you: its path, input size, input layout, model type, and label map.

To do it by hand instead, copy the model's file into `/opt/traffic-monitor/frigate/config/model_cache/` over SSH, and set `path: /config/model_cache/<file>` in the `model:` section. Unlike a `plus://` model, it also needs the keys that describe it: `width`, `height`, `input_tensor`, `input_pixel_format`, `input_dtype`, `model_type`, and `labelmap_path`. Frigate's [reference config](https://docs.frigate.video/configuration/advanced/reference) lists their values. The model must suit the device's detector, as a Frigate+ model must.

### What the installer keeps

Running the installer with `-f` replaces Frigate's config with a fresh copy, but keeps the `model:` section you chose, however you set it, as long as it isn't the installer's own model. Comments inside the section are lost. After you change the accelerator, a kept model may not suit the new one, and the Status page says so. [What `-f` replaces](https://docs.trafficmonitor.ai/dev/reference/tmsetup/#what-f-replaces) and [Add an accelerator later](https://docs.trafficmonitor.ai/dev/reference/tmsetup/#add-an-accelerator-later) have the details.

### The Frigate+ check

The Status page's Configuration group has a **Frigate+** check. It compares the key with the `model:` section of Frigate's config and says whether Frigate could use the model:

| Status       | Meaning                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                        |
| ------------ | ------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------ |
| Passed       | Frigate+ isn't in use: no key and no Frigate+ model. Or Frigate runs the Frigate+ model the config names. Without a key, it runs from the files on the device, and you can't submit snapshots.                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                 |
| Warning      | A key is set, but Frigate runs the installer's model, its own default model (on a device with no `model:` section), or one of your own. Snapshots can be submitted. Once Frigate+ has trained a model, set it as in [Use a model](#use-a-model).                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                               |
| Problem      | Frigate can't use the Frigate+ model the config names. Either no key is set and the model's files aren't on the device, so Frigate can't download it (**Set the key** opens the Frigate+ API key section of the Detection page), or the model isn't built for the device's detector; where Frigate's log says why, the check quotes it. Also a problem: the model id has characters an id can't have, or Frigate isn't answering and its log has an error, which the check quotes. When Frigate+ gave Frigate no token for the key, as with a wrong key, the check says so, and **Set the key** opens the Frigate+ API key section of the Detection page. See [If Frigate stops over a model](#if-frigate-stops-over-a-model). |
| Couldn't run | Frigate's config is missing or isn't valid YAML, or Frigate isn't answering and its log has no error to quote. Or Frigate is in safe mode for a reason other than the model, so whether it can use the model is unknown; the Apps group's **Frigate** check says why.                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                          |

When Frigate can't use its config, for example because of a model built for another detector, it starts in safe mode: it answers and looks healthy, but has no cameras and counts nothing. The Apps group's **Frigate** check reports that as a problem, whatever the cause, and quotes Frigate's messages. Fix the config in Frigate's configuration editor, then choose **Save & Restart**.

### If Frigate stops over a model

Frigate refuses a model it can't fetch when you save, so it ends up with one only in ways that skip that check:

- you edit Frigate's `config.yml` over SSH,
- the installer keeps the `model:` section with `-f` after the key was removed, or
- the key is removed or changed while the model's files aren't on the device yet.

Frigate then fails each time it starts, restarts every few seconds, and counts nothing. On the Status page, Frigate's row in the Services group says it restarted after failures, and the **Frigate** and **Frigate+** checks quote the last error in Frigate's log.

To get Frigate running again, do one of these:

1. On the Detection page, under **Other models on this device**, choose [**Use**](https://docs.trafficmonitor.ai/dev/use/detection/#use-a-model) on **The installer's model** (on a device without a Coral, on **Frigate's built-in model**). While Frigate isn't answering, the device edits Frigate's config itself and restarts Frigate.
1. Enter the right key on the Detection page, under [Frigate+](https://docs.trafficmonitor.ai/dev/use/detection/#frigate-plus). Saving it restarts Frigate, which then fetches the model.
1. Upload the model's two files on the Detection page, as in [A device without internet](#a-device-without-internet), and choose **Use**.
1. As a last resort, over SSH, open Frigate's config as root with `sudo nano /opt/traffic-monitor/frigate/config/config.yml` and replace its `model:` section with the installer's. Copy it from the [default Frigate config](https://github.com/glossyio/traffic-monitor/blob/main/container/frigate/config/config.yml.j2), where its `path` names the `.tflite` file in `model_cache`, or from a backup beside the file, if an earlier run of the installer with `-f` left one. Only a device with a Coral has that section; on another device, delete the `model:` section. Then restart Frigate with `sudo systemctl restart frigate.service`.

Running the installer with `-f` doesn't help, because it keeps the `model:` section.

Info

A wrong key on its own never stops Frigate. When it starts, Frigate contacts Frigate+ only to download a model whose files are missing, so a model whose files are on the device keeps running whatever the key.
# Reference

# config.yml settings

The Traffic Monitor's own settings live in `/opt/traffic-monitor/node-red-tm/config/config.yml` on the device. The installer writes it from [this template](https://github.com/glossyio/traffic-monitor/blob/main/container/node-red-tm/config/config.yml.j2) on the first install and leaves it alone afterwards, unless you run the installer with `-f`.

The Traffic Monitor reads the file again whenever you save it, so changes take effect without a restart. If the file has a YAML error, it keeps the previous settings until the service restarts, and after a restart it has no settings at all until you fix the file.

Keep the three top-level sections (`thingsboard`, `deployment`, `sensors`) in the file. The file has no time settings: the installer's `-z` option sets the device's time zone, and you change it later on the [Date and time](https://docs.trafficmonitor.ai/dev/use/device-health/#the-date-and-time-page) page. A `time` section left from an older install is ignored. The Default column below shows the values the template writes. A setting that's missing from the file behaves differently in a few cases:

- A camera or radar without `enabled` is off.
- A radar without `opt_api_commands_array` gets no extra commands.
- ThingsBoard without `host` stays off.
- A camera whose `camera_radar` names a radar that isn't in the file records no events. On a device without a radar, remove `camera_radar` or keep the radar's entry with `enabled: false`.

## thingsboard

Uploads events, readings, and device telemetry to a [ThingsBoard](https://thingsboard.io/) server. See [MQTT and ThingsBoard](https://docs.trafficmonitor.ai/dev/data-and-payloads/integrations/index.md).

| Setting    | Type              | Default                         | Meaning                                                                                                                          |
| ---------- | ----------------- | ------------------------------- | -------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- |
| `enabled`  | `true` or `false` | `false`                         | Turn the upload on.                                                                                                              |
| `host`     | text              | `tb.server.com` (a placeholder) | The server's hostname. If it starts with `http://` or `https://`, that is used and `protocol` is ignored. Required when enabled. |
| `protocol` | `http` or `https` | `https`                         | How to reach the server.                                                                                                         |
| `port`     | number            | none                            | Set it only if the server isn't on the standard port for the protocol.                                                           |

The device's access token isn't in this file. Set it on the control app's [Device page](https://docs.trafficmonitor.ai/dev/use/device-health/#tokens-and-keys); it's kept with the device's other secrets.

## deployment

Where the device is. Every event and reading is stored with a deployment id that points at these values. The control app's [Location page](https://docs.trafficmonitor.ai/dev/use/location/index.md) writes them when you claim the device, deploy it to a place, change the precision, or correct a value, so you rarely edit them here. All of them are optional.

| Setting              | Type                                                  | Default | Meaning                                                                                                                                                                                                                                          |
| -------------------- | ----------------------------------------------------- | ------- | ------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------ |
| `survey_id`          | `<8 lower-case hex digits>-si`, such as `3f9a1c2e-si` | empty   | The place in use, with no coordinates in it. The Location page writes it. Each device makes its own ids, and two devices never need to share one. Upper case is folded to lower case; an id in any other form is ignored and logged as an error. |
| `database_precision` | `none`, `1`, or `2`                                   | `'2'`   | How many decimal places of `lat` and `lon` the database keeps: `none` stores no coordinates, `1` about 10 km, `2` about 1 km. A number without quotes works too.                                                                                 |
| `lat`                | decimal degrees, such as `45.52252`                   | empty   | Latitude of the place in use, optional, with five decimal places at most. The database stores it rounded to `database_precision`; this file and the control app keep the exact value.                                                            |
| `lon`                | decimal degrees, such as `-122.69120`                 | empty   | Longitude, optional, with the same rules as `lat`. Set both or neither: a row with only one gets neither.                                                                                                                                        |
| `bearing`            | `n`, `s`, `e`, `w`, `ne`, `nw`, `se`, or `sw`         | empty   | The compass direction the camera and radar face. Optional; a value that isn't one of these, including one with spaces around it, is logged as an error.                                                                                          |

A change of `survey_id`, or of a sensor's `bearing`, closes that sensor's current deployment and starts a new one. A change of `lat` or `lon` doesn't. While `survey_id` is empty, current deployments stay as they are, and a bearing change waits until you set one. When you first set `survey_id`, a current deployment with no survey id and the same bearing takes it over and keeps its deployment id.

Lowering `database_precision` rewrites the current deployments in place. Raising it takes effect from the next new deployment, because coordinates already rounded can't be made finer. The Location page can also round the rows already stored; see [Choose the precision](https://docs.trafficmonitor.ai/dev/use/location/#choose-the-precision).

A `deployment:` block under a camera or radar can hold `bearing`, for a device whose cameras face different ways. A `lat` or `lon` there isn't read, because the location belongs to the whole device. The installer removes it, and the Status page's Location check warns about it until then.

### Edit the location by hand

Use the [Location page](https://docs.trafficmonitor.ai/dev/use/location/index.md) to move the device or fix a value. If you edit this section by hand instead, Node-RED applies the change as soon as you save the file, and the control app records it the next time it's opened, on its home page, Status page, or Location page:

- **`survey_id` set to a place the page lists** is a move there. The file takes that place's location, replacing any `lat` or `lon` you changed in the same edit. Node-RED starts the new deployments as soon as you save, at the location the file held then, and the control app gives them the place's location when it records the move. If the place has no location, those deployments keep the one the file held.
- **`survey_id` set to an id the page doesn't list** becomes a new place, in use, at this file's `lat` and `lon`.
- **Only `lat` or `lon` changed** is a correction of the place in use, as **Correct location** would be: the place's stored rows take the new location.
- **`survey_id` emptied**, as `tmsetup.sh -f` leaves it, is put back: the control app writes the place in use's id into the file again, and gives each sensor with an empty bearing the way it faces at that place. A bearing you set stays. `database_precision` goes back to the last value the control app saw while the file named a place, because after a reset the file holds the template's `'2'`. A coarser value you typed into the reset file stays. To choose a finer one, use the Location page, or edit the file once `survey_id` is back. If the place has a location, `lat` and `lon` get it back, whatever the file holds, because after a reset they come from the installer, not from you; correct a place's location on the Location page. If the place has none, a location in the file is a correction, as above. A typo stays as you typed it.
- **`lat` and `lon` both emptied**, when the place in use has a location, are put back too, because a place's location can be corrected but not removed. To keep the location out of the database, choose **No location stored** as the [precision](https://docs.trafficmonitor.ai/dev/use/location/#choose-the-precision).
- **A `lat` or `lon` that isn't a number in range**, such as one with a typo, stays in the file as you typed it. New deployments store no location until you fix it, and the Status page's Location check names the key.

On a device upgraded from a release that recorded coordinates, the update leaves `survey_id` empty, and the control app fills it in the first time it's opened after Node-RED has started; see [Places after an update](https://docs.trafficmonitor.ai/dev/build-your-own-device-diy/update/#places-after-an-update).

## sensors.cameras

One entry per camera, named exactly as the camera is named in Frigate. The default camera is `picam_h265`. Events from a camera that isn't listed here, or is disabled, are ignored.

To rename a camera, rename it in Frigate's config and choose **Save & Restart**. Frigate uses a new camera name only after it restarts, so **Save** alone changes nothing yet. Then rename its entry here to match. Until both names agree, that camera's events aren't recorded, and the Status page's **Cameras in config.yml** check shows an error.

| Setting            | Type                               | Default                   | Meaning                                                                                                                           |
| ------------------ | ---------------------------------- | ------------------------- | --------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- |
| `enabled`          | `true` or `false`                  | `true` for `picam_h265`   | Record this camera's events. Frigate keeps running either way.                                                                    |
| `camera_radar`     | a radar name from `sensors.radars` | `TM_RADAR_SERIAL_PORT_00` | The radar that supplies speeds for this camera. One radar can serve several cameras. Leave it out on a device without a radar.    |
| `plate_recognizer` | `true` or `false`                  | `false`                   | Send this camera's events to the [Plate Recognizer](https://docs.trafficmonitor.ai/dev/add-ons/plate-recognizer/index.md) add-on. |
| `deployment`       | block                              | inherited                 | Per-camera `bearing`.                                                                                                             |

## sensors.radars

One entry per radar. A radar's name is the name of the variable that holds its serial port in [node-red-tm.env](https://docs.trafficmonitor.ai/dev/configuration/environment/index.md), `TM_RADAR_SERIAL_PORT_00` through `TM_RADAR_SERIAL_PORT_03`.

| Setting                  | Type                     | Default                              | Meaning                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                        |
| ------------------------ | ------------------------ | ------------------------------------ | -------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- |
| `enabled`                | `true` or `false`        | `true` for `TM_RADAR_SERIAL_PORT_00` | Read this radar. Set it to `false` on a device without a radar.                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                |
| `opt_api_commands_array` | a JSON array in a string | `'["^/+0.00\n", "^/-0.00\n"]'`       | Extra [OPS243 API](https://omnipresense.com/wp-content/uploads/2023/06/AN-010-Y_API_Interface.pdf) commands sent to the radar when the service starts and whenever you save this file, after the Traffic Monitor's own setup commands. The default sets the cosine correction to 0 degrees in both directions. |
| `deployment`             | block                    | inherited                            | Per-radar `bearing`.                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                           |

## sensors.airquality_monitors

One entry per [air quality sensor](https://docs.trafficmonitor.ai/dev/add-ons/air-quality/index.md), named as the middle part of the topic the sensor publishes to: `aq/<name>/readings`.

| Setting               | Type              | Default    | Meaning                                                                                 |
| --------------------- | ----------------- | ---------- | --------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- |
| `enabled`             | `true` or `false` | `false`    | Record this sensor's readings. Readings from a sensor that isn't enabled are dropped.   |
| `mqtt_topic_incoming` | text              | `readings` | Present in the template but not used. The device subscribes to every topic under `aq/`. |

## addons.plate_recognizer

Only needed with the [Plate Recognizer](https://docs.trafficmonitor.ai/dev/add-ons/plate-recognizer/index.md) add-on. The section isn't in the template; add it.

| Setting | Type | Default | Meaning                                                                 |
| ------- | ---- | ------- | ----------------------------------------------------------------------- |
| `url`   | URL  | none    | The add-on's address inside the device, `http://plate-recognizer:8080`. |

The API token and license key aren't in this file. Set them on the control app's [Device page](https://docs.trafficmonitor.ai/dev/use/device-health/#tokens-and-keys); plates aren't read until they're set.

______________________________________________________________________

## description: The variables in node-red-tm.env and frigate.env: radar serial ports, database path, MQTT broker, the Frigate+ key, and the values the installer fills in.

# Env file settings

Two env files hold the environment that the Node-RED and Frigate containers start with. The installer writes each from its template on the first install and leaves it alone afterwards, unless you run the installer with `-f`. Most devices never need either edited.

## node-red-tm.env

`/opt/traffic-monitor/node-red-tm/node-red-tm.env` is written from [this template](https://github.com/glossyio/traffic-monitor/blob/main/container/node-red-tm/node-red-tm.env.j2).

After editing it, restart the service:

```
sudo systemctl restart node-red-tm.service
```

After changing the MQTT broker login

A restart or reboot isn't enough after you change `TM_MQTT_BROKER_USERNAME` or `TM_MQTT_BROKER_PASSWORD`. Run the installer instead, so Frigate gets the same login and port 1883 opens or closes to match:

```
bash traffic-monitor/script/tmsetup.sh -t node-red-tm
```

Otherwise the broker refuses Frigate's connection, and no events are recorded.

| Variable                                               | Default                          | Meaning                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                           |
| ------------------------------------------------------ | -------------------------------- | --------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- |
| `TM_VERSION`                                           | the installed release            | The Traffic Monitor version, shown on the dashboards and sent with telemetry. The installer sets it; don't edit it.                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                               |
| `TM_RPI_SN`                                            | the Raspberry Pi's serial number | Identifies the device in ThingsBoard, and fills `deviceName` in [deployment](https://docs.trafficmonitor.ai/dev/data-and-payloads/data-overview/#deployment) records. Set by the installer.                                                                                                                                                                                       |
| `TM_HOSTNAME`                                          | the device's hostname at install | Prefix for the file names of [data exports](https://docs.trafficmonitor.ai/dev/ui/database/index.md). Set by the installer.                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                       |
| `NODE_RED_CREDENTIAL_SECRET`                           | `myNodeRED1234`                  | Encrypts the credentials saved in the Node-RED editor. Leave it as it is: every installer run copies in the repository's credentials file, which is encrypted with this default, so a changed value leaves Node-RED unable to read it.                                                                                                                                            |
| `TM_NR_TOKEN_KEY`                                      | generated on the device          | Lets the Node-RED editor check that the device's [login](https://docs.trafficmonitor.ai/dev/use/control-app/index.md) let you in. The installer sets it on every run; leave it. Without it, the editor refuses everyone.                                                                                                                                                          |
| `TM_THINGSBOARD_ACCESS_TOKEN`                          | the token you set, or empty      | The device's access token for the [ThingsBoard upload](https://docs.trafficmonitor.ai/dev/data-and-payloads/integrations/#thingsboard). The installer fills it from the device's secrets on every run; change it on the [Device page](https://docs.trafficmonitor.ai/dev/use/device-health/#tokens-and-keys), not here. Empty keeps the upload off.                               |
| `TM_PLATE_RECOGNIZER_TOKEN`                            | the token you set, or empty      | The API token for the [Plate Recognizer](https://docs.trafficmonitor.ai/dev/add-ons/plate-recognizer/index.md) add-on. Filled and changed the same way. Empty keeps plate reads off.                                                                                                                                                                                              |
| `TM_INTERNAL_TOKEN`                                    | generated on the device          | Lets the control app read Node-RED's state for the [Status page](https://docs.trafficmonitor.ai/dev/use/device-health/#the-status-page). The installer sets it on every run; leave it. Without it, the Status page can't read Node-RED's state.                                                                                                                                   |
| `TM_DATABASE_PATH_TMDB`                                | `/db/tmdb.sqlite`                | The database, as seen inside the container. On the device it's `/opt/traffic-monitor/node-red-tm/db/tmdb.sqlite`. Leave it; schema migrations and downloads expect this path.                                                                                                                                                                                                     |
| `TM_MQTT_BROKER_HOST`                                  | `localhost`                      | The MQTT broker that Node-RED hosts. Frigate and the air quality sensor publish to it. See [MQTT and ThingsBoard](https://docs.trafficmonitor.ai/dev/data-and-payloads/integrations/index.md).                                                                                                                                                                                    |
| `TM_MQTT_BROKER_PORT`                                  | `1883`                           | The broker's port.                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                |
| `TM_MQTT_BROKER_USERNAME`                              | empty                            | The broker's login username. When it and the password are both set, the broker requires the login from every client, and port 1883 opens to the network. Letters, digits, `.`, `_`, and `-` only, with no quotes and no comment after the value. See [Connect from other devices](https://docs.trafficmonitor.ai/dev/data-and-payloads/integrations/#connect-from-other-devices). |
| `TM_MQTT_BROKER_PASSWORD`                              | empty                            | The broker's login password, with the same rules as the username.                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                 |
| `TM_RADAR_SERIAL_PORT_00` to `TM_RADAR_SERIAL_PORT_03` | `/dev/ttyACM0` to `/dev/ttyACM3` | The serial port of each radar. The variable's name is the radar's name in [config.yml](https://docs.trafficmonitor.ai/dev/configuration/node-red-config/#sensorsradars). The installer passes only the ports that exist at install time into the container, so after plugging in a radar rerun `bash traffic-monitor/script/tmsetup.sh -t node-red-tm`.                           |

## frigate.env

`/opt/traffic-monitor/frigate/frigate.env` is written from [this template](https://github.com/glossyio/traffic-monitor/blob/main/container/frigate/frigate.env.j2). After editing it, restart Frigate with `sudo systemctl restart frigate.service`.

| Variable                | Default                   | Meaning                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                              |
| ----------------------- | ------------------------- | -------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- |
| `FRIGATE_RTSP_PASSWORD` | `password`                | A password for cameras of your own: Frigate fills in `{FRIGATE_RTSP_PASSWORD}` in a camera's input path. The Traffic Monitor's own camera doesn't use it. The installer leaves it as you set it, unless you run it with `-f`.                                                                                                                                        |
| `PLUS_API_KEY`          | the key you set, or empty | The [Frigate+](https://docs.trafficmonitor.ai/dev/configuration/frigate-config/#better-models) API key. The installer fills it from the device's secrets on every run; change it on the [Detection page](https://docs.trafficmonitor.ai/dev/use/detection/#frigate-plus), not here. Empty means no key: Frigate can't submit snapshots or download a Frigate+ model. |

The other lines are the installer's. Leave them as they are:

- `FRIGATE_GO2RTC_RTSP_USER` and `FRIGATE_GO2RTC_RTSP_PASSWORD`: the login Frigate reads the device's camera stream with.
- `FRIGATE_PROXY_AUTH_SECRET`: lets Frigate trust who the device's [login](https://docs.trafficmonitor.ai/dev/use/control-app/index.md) says you are.
- `FRIGATE_MQTT_USER` and `FRIGATE_MQTT_PASSWORD`: Frigate's login to the MQTT broker, which follows the broker login in `node-red-tm.env`.
- `FRIGATE_HOME_DIR`, `FRIGATE_VERSION`, and `FRIGATE_BASE_PATH`: where Frigate's files are, its version, and the `/frigate/` path it's served at.

# Network ports

Other computers reach the Traffic Monitor's apps through the [home page](https://docs.trafficmonitor.ai/dev/use/home-page/index.md) on port 80. The apps themselves, and the control app on port 8090, listen only on the device itself (loopback). The ports in the table below are the ones other computers can reach.

| Port       | Used for                                                                                                                                                                               |
| ---------- | -------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- |
| 22         | SSH                                                                                                                                                                                    |
| 80         | The [control app](https://docs.trafficmonitor.ai/dev/use/control-app/index.md) and every app behind its login                                                                          |
| 1883       | MQTT, only when the broker has a login. See [MQTT and ThingsBoard](https://docs.trafficmonitor.ai/dev/data-and-payloads/integrations/#mqtt).                                           |
| 5353 (UDP) | `<hostname>.local` names (mDNS)                                                                                                                                                        |
| 8554       | The camera stream (RTSP), with a username and password                                                                                                                                 |
| 9090       | [Cockpit](https://docs.trafficmonitor.ai/dev/use/system-admin/#cockpit), with your Raspberry Pi login. The home page's Cockpit tile opens it, and it works when the home page doesn't. |

## The hotspot

When the device's Wi-Fi isn't on a network it knows, it runs a [hotspot](https://docs.trafficmonitor.ai/dev/use/wifi-hotspot/index.md) on the built-in radio (`wlan0`). The control app's [Network page](https://docs.trafficmonitor.ai/dev/use/wifi-hotspot/#the-network-page) shows the device's own addresses.

|         |                                                                                                                                                                                                                             |
| ------- | --------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- |
| Address | The device is `10.42.0.1`, on the network `10.42.0.0/24`. The address is fixed.                                                                                                                                             |
| DHCP    | The device gives each phone an address in that network.                                                                                                                                                                     |
| DNS     | The device answers every name with its own address, so a phone's connection test lands on the device and opens the control app's sign-in window.                                                                            |
| Ports   | The same as on your network, in the table above.                                                                                                                                                                            |
| Reach   | A phone on the hotspot reaches only the device. A firewall rule drops anything that would pass from the hotspot to another network, or back, so the hotspot has no internet and doesn't open your wired network to a phone. |

A request that reaches the device on the hotspot's address with any other name, such as the one a phone's connection test uses, gets a redirect to `http://10.42.0.1/`. A request for `10.42.0.1` or for the device's own name is answered as usual.

Whenever the device has a network, NetworkManager asks `connectivity-check.ubuntu.com` every 5 minutes whether the internet is reachable. The Status page's Internet check shows the answer. When an administrator [tests a Wi-Fi network](https://docs.trafficmonitor.ai/dev/use/wifi-hotspot/#put-the-unit-on-a-wi-fi-network) from the Network page, the device asks that network's DNS server for the address of `connectivity-check.ubuntu.com` (up to three times, a second apart) and makes one request to it through that network, to report whether the internet is reachable there.

## Camera stream login

The camera stream on port 8554 needs the username `frigate` and a password generated on the device at install. To play the stream in another program, such as VLC, read the password on the device:

```
sudo cat /etc/traffic-monitor/secrets/go2rtc_rtsp_password
```

Then open `rtsp://frigate:<password>@<device>:8554/picam_h265_detect`.

# Installer options

`script/tmsetup.sh` in the repository installs and updates the Traffic Monitor. Run it from the device, or from another computer with `-H`. [Install the software](https://docs.trafficmonitor.ai/dev/software-installation/index.md) and [Update the software](https://docs.trafficmonitor.ai/dev/build-your-own-device-diy/update/index.md) show the usual runs.

```
bash traffic-monitor/script/tmsetup.sh [flags]
```

## Flags

| Flag             | Meaning                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                     |
| ---------------- | ----------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- |
| `-h`             | Show the usage text and exit.                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                               |
| `-y`             | Answer yes to every prompt, including the reboot.                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                           |
| `-v`             | Verbose output. Repeat for more.                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                            |
| `-f`             | Replace the user-editable settings files with fresh copies from the templates. See [What `-f` replaces](#what-f-replaces).                                                                                                                                                                                                                                  |
| `-t TAG`         | Run one component, plus anything that has to change with it. Repeat for several. See [Tags](#tags).                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                         |
| `-T`             | List the tags and exit.                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                     |
| `-C NAME[,NAME]` | Turn on an optional component: `plate_recognizer` (see [Plate Recognizer](https://docs.trafficmonitor.ai/dev/add-ons/plate-recognizer/index.md)), or `mqtt_lan`, which creates an MQTT broker login when there isn't one (see [Connect from other devices](https://docs.trafficmonitor.ai/dev/data-and-payloads/integrations/#connect-from-other-devices)). |
| `-u`             | Also upgrade the operating system's packages (`apt full-upgrade`).                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                          |
| `-d PATH`        | Install folder. Default `/opt/traffic-monitor`. The docs assume the default.                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                |
| `-o USER`        | Owner of the installed files and processes. Default `tmadmin`, created by the installer.                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                    |
| `-g GROUP`       | Group of the installed files. Default `tmadmin`.                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                            |
| `-w CODE`        | The Wi-Fi country, a two-letter code such as `US` or `GB`. Without it, the installer asks when the device has none and the run includes the `wifi` tag; with `-y` or a remote run it keeps the device's country, or sets `US` when there is none. See [The Wi-Fi country](https://docs.trafficmonitor.ai/dev/use/wifi-hotspot/#the-wi-fi-country).          |
| `-z TIMEZONE`    | Time zone for the system and the dashboards, as a [tz database name](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_tz_database_time_zones). Default `America/Los_Angeles`.                                                                                                                                                                                          |
| `-L PATH`        | Where to write the installer's log.                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                         |
| `-a ARG`         | Pass an extra argument to the underlying Ansible run, without its leading hyphen.                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                           |

Remote runs:

| Flag             | Meaning                                                                                                                 |
| ---------------- | ----------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- |
| `-H HOST[,HOST]` | Install to these devices over SSH instead of the local machine. Separate several with commas.                           |
| `-l USER`        | The SSH username on the devices.                                                                                        |
| `-k`             | Ask for the SSH password.                                                                                               |
| `-K`             | Ask for the password for administrator rights (sudo). Needed on Raspberry Pi OS unless you've set up passwordless sudo. |

## Tags

Each tag reruns one part of the install. Without `-t`, everything runs. The pod, the reverse proxy, and the control app that checks every login have to change together, so the `podman`, `frigate`, `node-red-tm`, `go2rtc`, `revproxy`, and `tm-control` tags each update all three.

| Tag                | What it does                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                    |
| ------------------ | ----------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- |
| `base`             | Operating system packages, the owner account, and Cockpit. It runs with every `-t`.                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                             |
| `full_upgrade`     | The `apt full-upgrade`, when `-u` is given                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                      |
| `wifi`             | The Wi-Fi country, the [hotspot](https://docs.trafficmonitor.ai/dev/use/wifi-hotspot/index.md) (its profile, its password file, the firewall that keeps phones on it from reaching other networks, and the DNS that sends every name on it to the device), and the timer that moves the radio between a saved network and the hotspot. It sets the hotspot's password to the one in the password file, and never restarts a hotspot that is up. |
| `go2rtc`           | The camera streaming service on the host, and the stream login Frigate uses to read it                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                          |
| `detectors`        | Detects the Coral or Hailo accelerator, installs its driver, and writes the boot configuration. See [Add an accelerator later](#add-an-accelerator-later).                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                      |
| `podman`           | The container runtime and the pod                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                               |
| `frigate`          | Frigate's container, settings, and the devices it needs                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                         |
| `node-red-tm`      | Node-RED's container, flows, settings, and the radars it needs. Rerun it after plugging in a radar.                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                             |
| `plate-recognizer` | The optional Plate Recognizer container                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                         |
| `revproxy`         | The reverse proxy, with the home page built into its image                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                      |
| `tm-control`       | The [control app](https://docs.trafficmonitor.ai/dev/use/control-app/index.md) and its service, the `tm-control` command, the record of what was installed that the control app reads, and the setup code while the device isn't claimed. It also updates Frigate's `config.yml` from earlier versions: the stream login and the settings for the device's login.                                                                               |

## The device's card

When a run on the device ends while the device is unclaimed, the installer shows its **card** on the terminal: the setup code, and the hotspot's name and password. The card goes only to the terminal, so the hotspot's password stays out of the installer's log; the setup code is still in it. A run from another computer with `-H` prints a reminder only. `sudo tm-control card` prints the card on the device at any time.

## What `-f` replaces

Every run replaces the container images, service units, Node-RED flows, and the reverse proxy configuration. These files are kept unless you pass `-f`:
