## description: Add the Enviro+ air quality sensor to a Traffic Monitor: hardware, the sensor software, and the settings that connect it.

# Air quality sensor

The optional air quality sensor measures gases, particulate matter, temperature, pressure, humidity, and light. Readings go into the device's database every five minutes and appear on the legacy dashboard.

We make no warranty on the accuracy of the sensor or its data. If you have an environmental science background, we'd welcome your [help](https://docs.trafficmonitor.ai/dev/development/contributing/index.md).

## Hardware

The Pimoroni [Enviro+](https://www.pishop.us/product/enviro-for-raspberry-pi/) board with the Plantower [PMS5003](https://www.pishop.us/product/pms5003-particulate-matter-sensor-with-cable/) particulate matter sensor, connected to the Raspberry Pi's GPIO header with a [ribbon cable](https://docs.trafficmonitor.ai/dev/build-your-own-device-diy/recommended-hardware/#air-quality-sensor). The [assembly steps](https://docs.trafficmonitor.ai/dev/build-your-own-device-diy/assembly-instructions/#air-quality-sensor) show where the sensor sits in the enclosure. Pimoroni's [getting started guide](https://learn.pimoroni.com/article/getting-started-with-enviro-plus) covers the board itself.

## Sensor software

The sensor is read by [greendormer/enviroplus-monitor](https://github.com/greendormer/enviroplus-monitor), a Python service that runs on the Raspberry Pi and publishes readings to the device's MQTT broker. Install it following that repository's instructions, then set these keys in its `config.json` ([key reference](https://github.com/greendormer/enviroplus-monitor/blob/main/config_readme.md)):

| Key                               | Value                        | Why                                                                                                                                                                  |
| --------------------------------- | ---------------------------- | -------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- |
| `enable_send_data_to_homemanager` | `true`                       | Publish readings over MQTT                                                                                                                                           |
| `mqtt_broker_name`                | `"localhost"`                | The Traffic Monitor's broker, on port 1883                                                                                                                           |
| `mqtt_username`, `mqtt_password`  | The broker's login           | Needed once the broker has a login. See [Connect from other devices](https://docs.trafficmonitor.ai/dev/data-and-payloads/integrations/#connect-from-other-devices). |
| `indoor_outdoor_function`         | `"Outdoor"`                  | Use the outdoor topic                                                                                                                                                |
| `outdoor_mqtt_topic`              | `"aq/sensorname01/readings"` | The topic must start with `aq/`, and the middle part is the sensor's name in the Traffic Monitor's settings                                                          |
| `enable_display`                  | `false`                      | The board's screen is inside the enclosure                                                                                                                           |
| `long_update_delay`               | `300`                        | Seconds between readings                                                                                                                                             |

Set the location keys for your site as well. The software uses them to calibrate the pressure and gas readings for altitude, and to work out sunrise and sunset:

```
{
    "altitude": 49,
    "city_name": "Portland",
    "time_zone": "America/Los_Angeles",
    "custom_locations": [
        "Portland, United States of America, America/Los_Angeles, 45.52, -122.681944"
    ]
}
```

## Turn the sensor on in the Traffic Monitor

In `/opt/traffic-monitor/node-red-tm/config/config.yml`, under `sensors: airquality_monitors:`, set the sensor's entry to `enabled: true`. The entry's name must match the middle part of the MQTT topic:

```
sensors:
    airquality_monitors:
        sensorname01:
            enabled: true
```

The change takes effect when you save the file. Readings from a sensor that isn't enabled are dropped.

## What to expect

- The first readings arrive after the sensor's stabilization period, five minutes by default (`startup_stabilisation_time` in `config.json`).
- The gas readings are reported as uncalibrated for the first 100 minutes, while the gas sensor warms up.
- Readings show in the **Air Quality** section of the legacy dashboard at `http://<device>/ui/`, and are stored in the `airquality` table. [Air quality](https://docs.trafficmonitor.ai/dev/data-and-payloads/air-quality-aq-payload/index.md) describes the payload and the columns.
- The Raspberry Pi and the AI accelerator give off heat. The enclosure separates the sensor from them, but temperature and humidity may still read high.

# Plate Recognizer

Plate Recognizer is an optional add-on built on a commercial product from [Plate Recognizer](https://platerecognizer.com/), a company the Traffic Monitor project isn't affiliated with. It's off unless you install it. The add-on runs the company's on-device license plate reader in a container next to Frigate. For each `car` event from a camera you choose that passed through `zone_radar`, it reads the plate from Frigate's snapshot and stores the plate number, region, and vehicle make, model, and color.

Frigate has its own license plate recognition, which the Traffic Monitor doesn't turn on.

Danger

**Plates identify people.** With this add-on on, the database is no longer de-identified: the `plate_recognizer` table holds plate numbers. Keep the database on the device, don't share it, and make sure your use complies with local law. See [Data and privacy](https://docs.trafficmonitor.ai/dev/data-and-payloads/data-overview/index.md).

You need a Plate Recognizer account with an on-premise (SDK) license, which gives you an API token and a license key.

## Install

1. Run the installer with the add-on turned on:

   ```
   bash traffic-monitor/script/tmsetup.sh -C plate_recognizer
   ```

1. Enter your API token and license key on the control app's [Device page](https://docs.trafficmonitor.ai/dev/use/device-health/#tokens-and-keys), under **Tokens and keys**. Saving each one restarts the add-on.

1. Add the add-on's address to `/opt/traffic-monitor/node-red-tm/config/config.yml`, and turn the add-on on for each camera whose events should be read:

   ```
   sensors:
       cameras:
           picam_h265:
               enabled: true
               plate_recognizer: true

   addons:
       plate_recognizer:
           url: http://plate-recognizer:8080
   ```

   Node-RED picks up `config.yml` as soon as you save it, so it needs no restart.

1. Optionally, set `WORKERS` in `/opt/traffic-monitor/plate-recognizer/plate-recognizer.env` to the number of plates to read in parallel. `2` suits a Raspberry Pi 5. After you change it, restart the add-on with `sudo systemctl restart plate-recognizer.service`.

Upgrading a device that already reads plates

The installer moves a token and license key you typed into the add-on's env file, and a token in `config.yml`, to the device's secrets. Plate reads carry on without you entering them again. The Device page shows them as set.

Frigate's snapshots must stay on, which they are by default; the reader works from them.

## Data

Each read goes into the `plate_recognizer` table, keyed by the event it belongs to.

| Column                                                         | Type              | Meaning                                                                                               |
| -------------------------------------------------------------- | ----------------- | ----------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- |
| `event_id`                                                     | TEXT, primary key | The `id` of the [event](https://docs.trafficmonitor.ai/dev/data-and-payloads/events-payload/index.md) |
| `filename`                                                     | TEXT              | The snapshot that was read                                                                            |
| `timestamp`                                                    | TEXT              | The event's `frame_time`, when Frigate took the best frame of the car                                 |
| `camera_id`                                                    | TEXT              | Always `picam_h264`, whichever camera the event came from                                             |
| `processing_time`                                              | REAL              | Milliseconds the read took                                                                            |
| `plate_type`                                                   | TEXT              | Plate category, if the reader reports one                                                             |
| `plate_score`                                                  | REAL              | Confidence that a plate was found, 0 to 1                                                             |
| `plate_xmin`, `plate_ymin`, `plate_xmax`, `plate_ymax`         | INTEGER           | The plate's box in the snapshot, in pixels                                                            |
| `plate_value`                                                  | TEXT              | The plate number                                                                                      |
| `plate_value_score`                                            | REAL              | Confidence in the plate number, 0 to 1                                                                |
| `plate_region_value`                                           | TEXT              | The issuing region, such as `us-or`. The reader looks only for `us`, `us-or`, and `us-wa` plates.     |
| `plate_region_score`                                           | REAL              | Confidence in the region, 0 to 1                                                                      |
| `vehicle_type`                                                 | TEXT              | Vehicle category, such as `Sedan`                                                                     |
| `vehicle_score`                                                | REAL              | Confidence in the vehicle, 0 to 1                                                                     |
| `vehicle_xmin`, `vehicle_ymin`, `vehicle_xmax`, `vehicle_ymax` | INTEGER           | The vehicle's box in the snapshot, in pixels                                                          |
| `vehicle_make`, `vehicle_model`                                | TEXT              | Make and model                                                                                        |
| `vehicle_make_model_score`                                     | REAL              | Confidence in make and model, 0 to 1                                                                  |
| `vehicle_orientation`                                          | TEXT              | `Front`, `Rear`, or similar                                                                           |
| `vehicle_orientation_score`                                    | REAL              | Confidence in the orientation, 0 to 1                                                                 |
| `vehicle_color`                                                | TEXT              | Color                                                                                                 |
| `vehicle_color_score`                                          | REAL              | Confidence in the color, 0 to 1                                                                       |
| `json_payload`                                                 | TEXT              | The reader's full JSON response                                                                       |
# Ideas and use cases

# Ideas and use cases

The device collects more than counts. With extra zones in Frigate and the [event data](https://docs.trafficmonitor.ai/dev/data-and-payloads/events-payload/index.md), you can study how people and vehicles interact. Two examples follow; share yours in [Show and tell](https://github.com/glossyio/traffic-monitor/discussions/new?category=show-and-tell).

## Near misses at a crosswalk

A near miss is a driver and a vulnerable road user, such as a pedestrian at a crosswalk, in conflict at the same moment. These events are rarely captured today. The first step is a definition, and traffic law supplies one. As an example, Oregon's rules, summarized by [Portland Bicycle School](https://portlandbicycleschool.com/driving-around-bicycles/driving-around-pedestrians-faq/):

- Every corner is a crosswalk (ORS 801.220).
- A pedestrian has claimed the crossing as soon as any part of them, or their cane, wheelchair, or bicycle, enters it (ORS 811.028(4), 814.040(1)(a)).
- A driver must stay stopped until the pedestrian has cleared the driver's lane, or the lane they're turning into, plus one more lane (ORS 811.028).

To capture conflicts:

1. Mount the device with a view of the whole intersection.
1. Draw zones for the pedestrian areas and the driver areas.
1. Each `person` and `car` event then records its `start_time`, `end_time`, and `entered_zones`.
1. Download the data and look for a car entering a driver zone while a person was in the conflicting pedestrian zone.

For example, a person in `zone_ped_ne` about to cross south or west, and a car that enters `zone_intersection_e` and turns into `zone_intersection_n` before the person has crossed, is a near miss or at least an illegal turn. You can tighten the definition further: was the car stationary at the stop sign first, or did a pedestrian zone at the very edge of the sidewalk show intent to cross? A `person` and a `car` in the same road zone at the same time is the most serious case.

Zones for a near-miss study: pedestrian zones on each corner and intersection zones on each approach

## Vehicles that don't stop at a stop sign

A rolling stop, also called a California stop or Rhode Island stop, is a vehicle that passes a stop sign without stopping fully or for the required time. Some places let cyclists treat a stop sign as a yield (the [Idaho stop](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Idaho_stop)).

1. Mount the device high, looking down at the whole intersection.
1. In Frigate, draw a thin **stop-sign zone** across the road just before each stop sign, such as `zone_stop_sign_e` and `zone_stop_sign_w` for a two-way stop.
1. Give each stop-sign zone a [loitering time](https://docs.frigate.video/configuration/zones/#zone-loitering) that matches your jurisdiction, such as 3 seconds, and limit it to `car` if you like. The zone then appears in an event's `entered_zones` only if the vehicle stayed in it that long. A vehicle that rolled through has an event without the zone.
1. Optionally add wider zones for each approach, so you can also see turning movements: a car that went from `zone_intersection_e` to `zone_intersection_n` turned right.
1. Check the zones against a few real vehicles in Frigate's **Explore** view. It can take a while to find a car that stops properly.
# Help

# Troubleshooting and FAQ

## Troubleshooting

The dashboard shows no counts

Follow the checklist in [First-time setup](https://docs.trafficmonitor.ai/dev/setup-guide/#5-check-the-counts). The usual causes, in order: detection is off in Frigate, the objects don't pass through `zone_capture`, or the camera isn't enabled in `config.yml`.

Counts, but no speeds

The radar must be enabled in [config.yml](https://docs.trafficmonitor.ai/dev/configuration/node-red-config/#sensorsradars) and named in the camera's `camera_radar`, `zone_radar` must cover the road, and the device must be at a shallow angle to the traffic. If the radar was plugged in after the software was installed, rerun `bash traffic-monitor/script/tmsetup.sh -t node-red-tm` so the container can see it.

Frigate shows no camera image

Open **Camera feeds** from the home page, logged in as the administrator. If the `picam_h265_detect` stream plays there, the camera and its stream work, and the fault is between Frigate and the stream. Either the camera is off in Frigate's configuration editor, where `cameras: picam_h265:` needs `enabled: true`, or Frigate's video decoding is failing, which shows as ffmpeg errors in the `frigate.service` log. If the stream doesn't play, check the camera cable, then look at the `go2rtc_server.service` log in [System administration](https://docs.trafficmonitor.ai/dev/use/system-admin/index.md).

Detection is slow or misses objects

Without an AI accelerator, Frigate detects on the CPU and can't keep up with a busy road. [Hardware](https://docs.trafficmonitor.ai/dev/build-your-own-device-diy/recommended-hardware/#ai-accelerator) lists the supported accelerators. If you added one after installing, see [Add an accelerator later](https://docs.trafficmonitor.ai/dev/reference/tmsetup/#add-an-accelerator-later). With an accelerator, see [Tune object detection](https://docs.trafficmonitor.ai/dev/configuration/frigate-config/index.md).

The home page opens on a computer but not on an Android phone

On Android 17, an app needs permission to reach devices on your local network. Browsers that don't have it time out on every device on the phone's own Wi-Fi network, including your router's page, while other apps and computers reach the device. Open the browser's app settings (**Settings > Apps > Chrome**, for example), allow **Nearby devices** or local network access if it's listed, force-stop the browser, and open the page again. If the browser has no such setting, use a computer or another phone. On the device's own hotspot, use the phone's sign-in window instead: Android 17 browsers can't open the device there. See [Wi-Fi and the hotspot](https://docs.trafficmonitor.ai/dev/use/wifi-hotspot/#phones).

The hotspot doesn't show up on my phone

If its name is hidden, the phone doesn't list it. On Android, choose **Add network**, type the name, and tick **Hidden network**. See [Hide the name](https://docs.trafficmonitor.ai/dev/use/wifi-hotspot/#hide-the-name).

The first install seems stuck

Building Frigate's container image compiles ffmpeg on the device, which takes about 20 minutes with little output. Leave it running. The whole first install takes 30 minutes or more.

A database download fails

See [Data export](https://docs.trafficmonitor.ai/dev/ui/database/#download-the-database).

The Status page says the database schema is behind

Each time Node-RED starts, it updates the database's tables to the version the installed software expects. If an update fails, it's undone, and Node-RED runs on the old tables, where it may not be able to save new data. To see why it failed, run this over SSH or in Cockpit's terminal:

```
sudo journalctl -u node-red-tm | grep tmdb-migrate
```

If Node-RED started recently, the [diagnostics](https://docs.trafficmonitor.ai/dev/use/device-health/#download-diagnostics) on the Device page show the same lines. Restarting Node-RED tries the update again. If it fails again, [ask for help](https://docs.trafficmonitor.ai/dev/help-and-faq/where-can-i-get-support/index.md) and attach the diagnostics.

I edited config.yml and nothing changed

The Traffic Monitor reads the file again when you save it, so a change that doesn't take effect usually means a YAML error, such as a wrong indent or a missing space after a colon. The `node-red-tm.service` log in [System administration](https://docs.trafficmonitor.ai/dev/use/system-admin/index.md) shows the error. Fix the file before you restart the service; [config.yml settings](https://docs.trafficmonitor.ai/dev/configuration/node-red-config/index.md) explains why.

## Privacy

### What does the device record?

The database records what passed (a label such as `car`), when, how fast, and through which zones. It holds no images and no plate numbers with the default settings. Frigate keeps a cropped snapshot and a short clip of each detection for about an hour, so you can check what it saw, and you can turn that off. By default, the device sends no images or video anywhere: everything is processed on the device, and the database holds only metadata. The live view, the recordings, and Frigate's snapshots are behind the device's [login](https://docs.trafficmonitor.ai/dev/use/control-app/index.md), which decides who on your network can open the apps. It isn't a control on the images themselves: anyone with an account can see them, and they're ordinary files on the device's card. [Data and privacy](https://docs.trafficmonitor.ai/dev/data-and-payloads/data-overview/#privacy) explains, and lists the features that would change what's stored.

### Why this design?

The Traffic Monitor is built privacy-first because we believe in:

- **Ethical and transparent monitoring.** The code, the architecture, and the models are open, so anyone can see what the device does, and operators, especially public bodies, can be held to account.
- **Community safety and trust.** Detection runs on the device, nothing is sent to an outside server unless you set it up, and the data stays in your control.
- **Unbiased data collection.** Detection runs without human bias, but machine learning models can carry [algorithmic bias](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Algorithmic_bias). We use public-domain and open source models wherever possible and name the models in use.

To keep an area out of view, aim the camera so the area is out of frame. A motion mask doesn't hide it; see [Data and privacy](https://docs.trafficmonitor.ai/dev/data-and-payloads/data-overview/#privacy).

## Capacity

### How many objects can it track at once?

More than a busy street produces. The practical limit is objects hiding each other, as at the start of a race, where the camera can't see the person behind another.

The AI accelerator runs an inference in about 10 ms, which is about 100 inferences per second, and Frigate runs several inferences per frame when there's motion in several places. On a road with trees casting moving shadows, Frigate has been seen checking more than 18 motion regions and tracking 9 labeled objects at once, with inference time still around 9 ms. The video is decoded in hardware, and the CPU, which encodes the camera stream and runs motion detection, had headroom to spare. Frigate's discussions [#7491](https://github.com/blakeblackshear/frigate/discussions/7491) and [#18326](https://github.com/blakeblackshear/frigate/discussions/18326) explain how detections per frame are bounded.

A road where shadows produce many motion regions, all checked for objects

# Get support

The Traffic Monitor is a volunteer-run open source project. The community answers questions as it can, so please be patient, and help others when you can. Everyone follows the [Code of Conduct](https://github.com/glossyio/traffic-monitor/blob/main/CODE_OF_CONDUCT.md).

## Search first

Search these docs, then the [repository](https://github.com/glossyio/traffic-monitor): the search box at the top right covers discussions, issues, and code, with filters on the left.

## Chat

The [Traffic Monitor Zulip chat](https://trafficmonitor.zulipchat.com/) is the quickest place to ask a question, suggest an idea, or show a deployment. Developers discuss code there too, so it's also the place to start [contributing](https://docs.trafficmonitor.ai/dev/development/contributing/index.md).

## GitHub discussions

The [discussions board](https://github.com/glossyio/traffic-monitor/discussions) is for longer conversations:

- 💬 [General](https://github.com/glossyio/traffic-monitor/discussions/new?category=general): anything at all
- 💡 [Ideas](https://github.com/glossyio/traffic-monitor/discussions/new?category=ideas): feature ideas, and votes on them
- 🗳️ [Polls](https://github.com/glossyio/traffic-monitor/discussions/new?category=polls)
- 🙏 [Q&A](https://github.com/glossyio/traffic-monitor/discussions/new?category=q-a): ask for help
- 👐 [Show and tell](https://github.com/glossyio/traffic-monitor/discussions/new?category=show-and-tell): what you've built

## GitHub issues

Open an [issue](https://github.com/glossyio/traffic-monitor/issues) for a specific bug, a feature request, or a technical question that the discussions haven't answered. Include enough detail for someone else to reproduce or understand it.

- 🐞 [Bug report](https://github.com/glossyio/traffic-monitor/issues/new?assignees=&labels=&projects=&template=bug_report.md&title=)
- 💡 [Feature request](https://github.com/glossyio/traffic-monitor/issues/new?assignees=&labels=&projects=&template=feature_request.md&title=)

An issue may be closed without a full resolution, for example as a duplicate, after inactivity, or because the work is tracked elsewhere. That isn't a lack of interest; comment or reopen if it still matters.

# Contributing

Thank you for your interest in getting involved! We welcome all skill levels and abilities as contributions. Visit our [Traffic Monitor GitHub](https://github.com/glossyio/traffic-monitor) page to get involved.

Contributions can include any of the following plus more!

- 💡 [Feature requests](https://github.com/glossyio/traffic-monitor/issues/new?assignees=&labels=&projects=&template=feature_request.md&title=) and use case ideas
- 🐞 [Bug reports](https://github.com/glossyio/traffic-monitor/issues/new?assignees=&labels=&projects=&template=bug_report.md&title=)
- 👩‍💻 [Code contributions](https://github.com/glossyio/traffic-monitor/blob/main/CONTRIBUTING.md), see Contributing
- 👍 Comment on or thumbs-up [milestones](https://github.com/glossyio/traffic-monitor/milestones) or [issues](https://github.com/glossyio/traffic-monitor/issues)
- 💬 Questions, comments, and videos/images of your deployments on our [Traffic Monitor Zulip Chat](https://trafficmonitor.zulipchat.com/)!

We foster a safe and welcoming community, review [our Code of Conduct](https://github.com/glossyio/traffic-monitor?tab=coc-ov-file#readme).

## Use of AI tools

You may use AI coding assistants to help draft, review, or explain a contribution, but you remain its author: understand and test every change you submit. Never share images, video clips, or plate reads with an AI tool, and use placeholders instead of real passwords, keys, or tokens. The de-identified `tmdb.sqlite` database may be shared only with the device operator's explicit consent, and never if plate recognition was ever enabled, because it then holds plate numbers. See [Use of AI tools](https://github.com/glossyio/traffic-monitor/blob/dev/CONTRIBUTING.md#use-of-ai-tools) in CONTRIBUTING.md for the details and for how to label AI-assisted commits.

## Writing docs

These docs are Markdown files in the repo's [`docs/`](https://github.com/glossyio/traffic-monitor/tree/dev/docs) folder, built with [Material for MkDocs](https://squidfunk.github.io/mkdocs-material/). Docs changes go in the same pull request as the code they describe, against `dev`.

- **Preview while you edit:** from the repo root, run `python3 -m venv ~/.venvs/tm-docs && ~/.venvs/tm-docs/bin/pip install --require-hashes -r docs-site/requirements.txt` once, then `~/.venvs/tm-docs/bin/mkdocs serve` and open <http://127.0.0.1:8000>.
- **Check before you push:** `mkdocs build --strict` fails on broken links, anchors, and images, and on pages missing from the nav. Pull requests run the same check.
- **New pages** go in the `nav:` list in `mkdocs.yml`, under the section for the reader's job (see below). A page outside the folders already listed under the `llmstxt` plugin also goes in that plugin's matching section, so AI tools can find it in `llms.txt`. Keep a page's file path when you move it in the nav; if the path must change, add the old path to the `moved` map in `docs-site/pages-root/404.html`.
- **Images** go in `docs/assets/images/`. Link them with Markdown, `![Alt text](../assets/images/name.png)`, so the build can check the path. Add a caption with `<figure markdown="span">` (see existing pages).
- **Callouts** use admonitions: `!!! info`, `!!! success`, `!!! warning`, or `!!! danger`, followed by the text indented four spaces.

Versions: pushes to `dev` publish to [`/dev/`](https://docs.trafficmonitor.ai/dev/), and each release tag (`vX.Y.Z`) publishes a frozen copy and becomes `/latest/`, the default version.

### Style

Aim for pages that are complete but quick to read: everything the reader needs, and nothing they don't. These rules apply to every docs change, whether a person or an AI tool drafted it.

- **One reader and one job per page.** Pages about installing, setup, configuration, the dashboards, and the data tell the person running a device what to do or what something means. Details for contributors go in the Development pages or in the README next to the code. [Diátaxis](https://diataxis.fr/) names the four jobs: tutorial, how-to guide, reference, and explanation. Use it to decide what belongs on the page you're editing, not to reorganize the site. The nav sections map to those jobs:

  | Section                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                             | Job                                            | Reader                                  |
  | ----------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- | ---------------------------------------------- | --------------------------------------- |
  | Get started                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                         | Explanation and orientation                    | Anyone new                              |
  | Build your own, Deploy, Add-ons                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                     | How-to guides, one task per page               | Someone building or installing a device |
  | Use the device                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                      | How-to guides for the running device           | Someone operating a device              |
  | Reference                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                           | Tables: every setting, flag, topic, and column | Someone looking a value up              |
  | Ideas and use cases, Help                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                           | Ideas, troubleshooting, and where to ask       | Someone curious or stuck                |
  | Development                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                         | Contributors                                   | You                                     |
  | \* **Leave out what the reader won't act on,** such as Ansible variables and task names, Node-RED node names, and files they won't open. Give real values, such as the default install folder `/opt/traffic-monitor`, instead of variables.                                         |                                                |                                         |
  | \* **Revise in place.** Rewrite the text your change affects and delete what it makes obsolete, rather than adding a paragraph. Keep the docs edit in proportion to the change; a diff that removes more than it adds is fine.                                                      |                                                |                                         |
  | \* **Describe how things work, not how they changed.** Don't narrate changes ("now supports", "new in", "previously"). Each release has its own copy of the docs, and history belongs in commit messages and release notes.                                                         |                                                |                                         |
  | \* **Say each fact once,** and link to it from other pages. Link to config files and code in the repo instead of copying them into a page, because copies go stale. Link to the `main` branch, which tracks the latest release, so the link matches `/latest/` rather than `/dev/`. |                                                |                                         |
  | \* **Put the common case first.** Move edge cases and troubleshooting into a collapsed callout (`???` instead of `!!!`), a table, or the [FAQ](https://docs.trafficmonitor.ai/dev/help-and-faq/frequently-asked-questions/index.md).                                                |                                                |                                         |
  | \* **Use tables for reference data,** with one row per setting or database column and its type, default, and meaning.                                                                                                                                                               |                                                |                                         |
  | \* **Keep the language plain:** "you", present tense, active voice, short sentences, and no filler such as "simply", "just", or "note that". Save callouts for what the reader must not miss.                                                                                       |                                                |                                         |
  | \* **Check every value against the code,** including defaults, paths, ports, and names.                                                                                                                                                                                             |                                                |                                         |

For anything these rules don't cover, follow the [Google developer documentation style guide](https://developers.google.com/style).

______________________________________________________________________

## description: Set up to change the Traffic Monitor: the Node-RED flows, the database schema, and testing on a dev Pi.

# Dev environment

The Traffic Monitor is open source, so you can change your devices to suit your needs. If others would benefit, [join the community](https://docs.trafficmonitor.ai/dev/help-and-faq/where-can-i-get-support/index.md) and [contribute back](https://docs.trafficmonitor.ai/dev/development/contributing/index.md).

The [repository](https://github.com/glossyio/traffic-monitor) is a monorepo with everything needed to run a device: the installer, the container definitions, the Node-RED flows, and these docs.

## Node-RED logic

[Node-RED](https://nodered.org/) runs the Traffic Monitor's logic: it receives events from Frigate and readings from the radar, pairs events with speeds, writes the database, serves the dashboards, and sends data on. The flows are in the repository at `container/node-red-tm/data/flows.json`, and the installer copies them to the device on every run, so changes made only in a device's editor are lost on the next update.

To develop on a device:

1. Log in to the device as the administrator, then open the Node-RED editor at `http://<device>/nr/`. The editor has no login of its own.
1. Create a new project and clone your fork of the repository. This replaces the flows on the device, so save any changes first.
1. Point the project's flow and package files at `container/node-red-tm/data/flows.json` and `package.json`, so your edits land in the repository's files.
1. Commit your changes to a branch of your fork.
1. Open a pull request, following [Contributing](https://docs.trafficmonitor.ai/dev/development/contributing/index.md).

## Database schema

The tables are defined by numbered SQL migrations in `container/node-red-tm/schema/migrations/`, not by the flows. Each time `node-red-tm.service` starts, it applies the migrations the database doesn't have yet, before Node-RED opens it. The `README.md` in the schema directory describes the whole process, from writing a migration to testing the upgrade on a Pi.

To change the schema:

1. Add the next numbered migration, regenerate `schema.sql`, and update the table docs under [Data](https://docs.trafficmonitor.ai/dev/data-and-payloads/data-overview/index.md).

1. Run the tests, using the dev environment from [Contributing](https://docs.trafficmonitor.ai/dev/development/contributing/index.md):

   ```
   .venv/bin/python -m pytest container/node-red-tm/schema/tests
   ```

To try a migration on a dev device, apply it while Node-RED is stopped. Deploying from the Node-RED editor doesn't restart the service, so it doesn't apply migrations. These commands use the default owner (`tmadmin`) and install folder, and run the migration script from your Node-RED project's clone:

```
sudo systemctl stop node-red-tm.service
sudo runuser -u tmadmin -- python3 \
    /opt/traffic-monitor/node-red-tm/data/projects/<project>/container/node-red-tm/schema/tmdb_migrate.py \
    --db /opt/traffic-monitor/node-red-tm/db/tmdb.sqlite
sudo systemctl start node-red-tm.service
```

The database records each migration it applies. If you change a migration after applying it, restore the copy saved in `/opt/traffic-monitor/node-red-tm/db/backup/` and apply it again.

## Control app

The control app in `tm-control/` serves the home page and the login in front of every app. [tm-control](https://docs.trafficmonitor.ai/dev/development/tm-control/index.md) describes its code, how the login reaches each app, and how to run it on a laptop without a Pi.

## Testing on a dev Pi

`script/devpi/tmdev.py` deploys your working copy to a bench Pi over SSH, runs commands on it, and records a PR's Pi test plan as a checklist. Every deploy, command, and check goes into a run log on your machine, so you can see later what ran on which Pi and how it went.

The Pis are defined in an inventory file that lists each Pi's address, login, and SSH key, plus the hardware it should have. That file and the run log stay on your machine, outside the repository. `script/devpi/README.md` covers setup and use.

Warning

Use these tools only with bench units, not field devices. Deploys pass `-y` to the installer, so the Pi reboots whenever the installer needs it.

______________________________________________________________________

## description: How the control app (tm-control) is built: its backend modules, the login check nginx runs for every app, the status checks, root jobs and polkit, fake mode, and how to add a module or a check.

# tm-control

`tm-control` is the device's control app: the home page, setup, the login in front of every app, the device's accounts, and the Status, Device, Date and time, Network, Detection, and Location pages. [Control app and login](https://docs.trafficmonitor.ai/dev/use/control-app/index.md), [Check and fix the device](https://docs.trafficmonitor.ai/dev/use/device-health/index.md), [Wi-Fi and the hotspot](https://docs.trafficmonitor.ai/dev/use/wifi-hotspot/index.md), [Choose the detection model](https://docs.trafficmonitor.ai/dev/use/detection/index.md), and [Places and location](https://docs.trafficmonitor.ai/dev/use/location/index.md) describe it from the operator's side. This page is for changing it.

It has three parts, all in the repository's [`tm-control/`](https://github.com/glossyio/traffic-monitor/tree/main/tm-control) folder:

| Folder     | What it is                                            | How it reaches the device                                                                                                           |
| ---------- | ----------------------------------------------------- | ----------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- |
| `backend/` | The Python app (FastAPI) and the `tm-control` command | Copied root-owned to `/usr/local/lib/traffic-monitor/tm-control`, with its own virtual environment, and run as `tm-control.service` |
| `ui/`      | The web pages (Vue 3, Vuetify 3, TypeScript, Vite)    | Built into the reverse proxy's image and served by nginx at `/`                                                                     |
| `jobs/`    | Scripts for the few things that need root             | Copied root-owned to `/usr/local/libexec/traffic-monitor/` and run by fixed systemd units                                           |

## How it runs

`tm-control.service` runs on the host, not in the pod, so the login keeps working when Podman doesn't. It runs as the code owner (default `tmadmin`), never as root, in a systemd sandbox, and listens on `127.0.0.1:8090` only. nginx is the only way in from the network.

It reads two things the installer writes, and keeps one database of its own:

- `/etc/traffic-monitor/secrets/`: two kinds of secret, and the hotspot's password. Five are generated once on the device: the session key, Frigate's proxy secret, the Node-RED editor's token key, the token for Node-RED's internal status, and go2rtc's RTSP password. Four are entered by an administrator: the ThingsBoard access token and the Plate Recognizer token and license key on the Device page, and the Frigate+ API key on the Detection page. The installer creates them empty, and only the `set-secret` job writes them. `GENERATED_SECRETS` and `ENTERED_SECRETS` in `core/secrets.py` match the role's `tmsetup_secret_names` and `tmsetup_entered_secret_names` (a test keeps each pair equal), `DEVICE_SECRETS` is the two together, and the diagnostics redact the value of each. An empty file means the secret isn't set. The `secrets` module (`GET /secrets`, and `POST` and `DELETE /secrets/{name}`) lists what is set, never a value, and starts the job. The hotspot's password, `hotspot_password`, is in neither list: `tm-hotspot-setup` creates it, and writes it again when it adopts a hand-made profile; otherwise only the `network` job changes it. tm-control reads it (`read_hotspot_password` in `core/secrets.py`) for one route, `GET /network/hotspot/password`, which answers admins only.
- `/etc/traffic-monitor/manifest.json`: what the installer installed and found, such as the version, the installing user, the proxied apps, the home page's colors, and, on a device with a Coral, the model section the installer gives Frigate (`frigate.coral_model`, from the role's `tmsetup_frigate_coral_model`), which the Detection page puts back, and `network`, the hotspot's Wi-Fi device, profile name, and address (`wlan0`, `tm-hotspot`, `10.42.0.1`, from the role's `tmsetup_wifi_device`, `tmsetup_hotspot_profile`, and `tmsetup_hotspot_address`), which the Network checks and `tm-control card` read.
- `/var/lib/tm-control/state.sqlite`: users, the claim and the setup code's hash, license acceptances, job records, an audit log, and the Location page's places (`surveys`, `survey_bearings`, and `survey_corrections`). Numbered migrations in `core/state.py` create and update it, recorded in `PRAGMA user_version`. Never change a migration that has shipped; add the next one.

While the device is unclaimed, the installer keeps the setup code in a root-only file, `/etc/traffic-monitor/setup-code`, and hands it to `tm-control set-setup-code` on every run, which stores only its hash. The installer's command-line steps run as the code owner, and `sudo tm-control reset-admin` drops to that user after writing a new code file, so root never writes the database.

## The login check

nginx checks every app path with `auth_request` before it proxies the request. Each app's location file includes one of two snippets, `auth-viewer.conf` (any logged-in user) or `auth-admin.conf` (administrators), which send a subrequest to tm-control's `GET /api/v1/auth/verify`:

```
browser ──GET /frigate/──▶ nginx (port 80)
                             │  auth_request /_auth  (internal location)
                             │    X-Original-URI: /frigate/
                             │    X-TM-Required-Role: viewer   (admin for /_auth_admin)
                             │    X-Forwarded-For: the browser's address
                             │    Cookie: tm_session=…
                             ▼
                           tm-control 127.0.0.1:8090  /api/v1/auth/verify
                             │
       ┌─────────────────────┼──────────────────────────┬──────────────────────────┐
       ▼                     ▼                          ▼                          ▼
  200 + identity       401 + X-TM-Redirect         403 forbidden        no answer (down, timeout)
  headers               (/setup, /login?next=…,     nginx returns 403    nginx returns 503 with
       │                 /welcome, or /waiting)                          the rescue page
       │                nginx answers 302
       ▼
  nginx proxies to the app, adding the headers that app needs
```

A 200 carries `X-TM-User`, `X-TM-Role`, `X-TM-Frigate-Secret`, and, for administrators, `X-TM-NR-Token`. The snippets copy them into nginx variables, and each app's location passes on what that app understands:

| App                                      | What nginx sends it                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                  |
| ---------------------------------------- | ------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------ |
| Frigate (`127.0.0.1:8971`)               | `X-Forwarded-User` and `X-Forwarded-Groups` (the role), and `X-Proxy-Secret`, which Frigate checks against `FRIGATE_PROXY_AUTH_SECRET` in `frigate.env`. nginx always sends both forwarded headers, because Frigate serves a request with only the secret as its default role, and it blanks `Remote-User`, `Remote-Groups`, and `Remote-Role`, which Frigate would also trust. Frigate's own login is off (`auth: enabled: false`). |
| Node-RED editor (`/nr/`)                 | `x-tm-nr-token`, a short-lived token that `settings.js` checks with `TM_NR_TOKEN_KEY` from `node-red-tm.env`. The editor has no users of its own.                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                    |
| Dashboards, camera feeds, data downloads | No identity: nginx's check is the whole gate.                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                        |

A few rules keep the check sound:

- Only nginx's internal `/_auth` and `/_auth_admin` locations may call verify. A `location ^~ /api/v1/auth/verify` returns 404 to the network, the `/api/` location clears `X-TM-Required-Role`, and verify answers 404 without that header.
- The check is always a `GET` without a body, and without the `Authorization` header, so no credential a client sends there reaches tm-control.
- Sessions last 7 days and roll: verify and the API re-issue a cookie that's more than a day old, and the snippets pass verify's `Set-Cookie` on to the browser. An app location must not set an `add_header` of its own, or it would drop that cookie.
- Only the check's own failure, which `auth_request` turns into a 500, becomes the rescue page (`error_page 500 =503 /unavailable.html`). An app's own 502 or 504 stays as it is.

The Node-RED token is `base64url(JSON {"u", "r", "exp"})`, a dot, and `base64url(HMAC-SHA256(key, first part))`, without padding, valid for 5 minutes. `NodeRedToken` in `backend/tm_control/core/auth.py` mints it, and `verifyProxyToken` in `container/node-red-tm/data/settings.js` checks it. Change both together; `script/tests/test_node_red_settings.py` runs tokens from one through the other.

The rest of the API, under `/api/v1/`, checks the session cookie itself. Every error has one shape, `{"error": {"code", "message", "detail"}}`. A request that changes something must send JSON from a page on the device (a matching `Origin` or `Referer`), or it gets 403.

### Download links

Android's sign-in window, which on Android 17 is the only browser that can reach a unit on its hotspot, fetches a download twice: its own request carries the session cookie, then it hands the address to a download helper that sends no cookie. So the Data export page asks for a link that passes the check once without the cookie:

1. Just before it starts a download, the page sends `POST /api/v1/auth/download-link` with `{"files": …}`. tm-control answers an administrator with `/storefiles?files=…&tm_token=…`, a random one-time token kept in memory. Anyone else gets an error, and the page falls back to the plain `/storefiles?files=…` address, which still works wherever the browser downloads the file itself.
1. The browser's own request has a session, so verify checks it as usual and leaves the link unused.
1. The helper's request has no session. verify lets it through as the administrator only when the address is exactly `/storefiles` with `files` and `tm_token` and nothing else, on an admin location, within 600 seconds, from the address the link was made for (`X-Forwarded-For`, which the `/_auth` locations set to nginx's own `$remote_addr`), and for the same `files`. The user must still be an administrator with the same sessions, and the current license agreement must be accepted. The answer carries `X-TM-User` and `X-TM-Role` only: no Frigate secret, no Node-RED token, no cookie.

The first request without a session that presents a token spends it, whether or not the rest matched. A login redirect leaves the token out of its `next=`. nginx's access log records the token; the parameter is named `tm_token` so that the diagnostics download hides its value with every other key ending in `token`. The two download templates live in `flows.json` (the ui-templates "Button to trigger download request" and "redirect to storefiles URL"), and `script/tests/test_node_red_flows.py` checks that they ask for the same link.

## Backend layout

```
tm-control/backend/tm_control/
  app.py         create_app(): loads the state, secrets, manifest, and license agreement, and mounts the modules
  cli.py         the tm-control command: serve, migrate, claim-status, set-setup-code, reset-admin, card,
                 and for development fake-reset and dump-openapi
  fake.py        fake mode's reset and the OpenAPI dump
  core/          shared rules: auth (passwords, sessions, backoff, setup code, users), csrf, errors, jobs,
                 card (the device's card), manifest, migrate (config updates for older installs), secrets, settings, state
  adapters/      the outside world: command (runs an argv list with a timeout and an output cap, never a shell),
                 systemd, timedate, sysinfo, hardware, network (nmcli and iw, read-only), the apps' HTTP APIs (frigate,
                 nodered, go2rtc), mqtt,
                 redact, yamlfile
  modules/       one folder per feature, each with a router: auth, setup, account, jobs, status, services, apps,
                 hardware, network, secrets, system, time, detection, location
```

Rules live in the backend; the UI shows what the API returns and posts what the operator types. `tm-control/ui/README.md` describes the UI's layout and design.

### Root jobs and polkit

tm-control never runs as root and never uses sudo. polkit lets its user do two things, both listed in `tmsetup_tm_control_polkit` in the role's `vars/main.yml`, and nothing else:

- Start, stop, and restart a fixed list of units. tm-control itself isn't on it; restart it with Cockpit or SSH. `tm-job-network.service` is on it for the Network page's changes, `tm-job-network-join.service` for a Wi-Fi join, `tm-network-retry.service` is on it for the Hotspot check's fix, and `FIX_UNITS` in `modules/services/units.py` lists the units like it, which a check's fix may start but the Services list doesn't show; `POST /services/{unit}/restart` accepts them.
- Seven actions: `org.freedesktop.timedate1.set-time`, `set-timezone`, and `set-ntp` for the Date and time page, and `org.freedesktop.login1.reboot`, `reboot-multiple-sessions`, `power-off`, and `power-off-multiple-sessions` for the Device page. The `-ignore-inhibit` variants aren't granted, so tm-control asks logind (`CanReboot`, `CanPowerOff`) first and answers 409 while an inhibitor, such as an update, holds the device up.

A time zone change restarts `traffic-monitor.service` and `revproxy.service` after the response, because the containers bind-mount `/etc/localtime` and keep the old zone until they restart. A time change that moved the clock ahead by more than 20 seconds (`FRIGATE_JUMP_SECONDS` in `modules/time/router.py`), by `set-time` or by NTP while the request watched, restarts `frigate.service` the same way, or at once when a later step of the request fails. Frigate's capture stops on such a step and, from a few minutes, may not recover by itself. A time zone change in the same request restarts the pod instead, which covers Frigate. Each admin action records an audit row. For work that needs root, tm-control writes a request to `/run/tm-control/jobs/<name>.json` and starts `tm-job-<name>.service`, a fixed root-owned oneshot unit. Its script in `tm-control/jobs/` checks the request strictly, does one thing, and deletes the request. tm-control follows the run through the unit and the journal, and `GET /api/v1/jobs/{id}` reports its status and log lines. There are four jobs:

| Job               | What it does                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                       |
| ----------------- | ------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------ |
| `system-password` | Sets the installing user's Linux password. It refuses an account that doesn't exist or has uid 0. `tmsetup.sh` also refuses to run as root, but a remote install with `-l root` still records root as the installing user, so the job's own check is the one that counts.                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                          |
| `set-secret`      | Writes or empties one entered secret. The request holds the secret's name and value. The script accepts only the four names in its own table (`thingsboard_access_token`, `frigate_plus_api_key`, `plate_recognizer_token`, and `plate_recognizer_license_key`), and only an empty value or one that matches that secret's pattern, and it refuses anything else without printing the value. It writes the secret's file, rewrites the secret's `KEY=` lines in `node-red-tm.env`, `frigate.env`, or `plate-recognizer.env`, then restarts the units that read them, in that order. A step that fails leaves the device no worse than before, and the log says which step it was. If a restart fails, the secret is already written, and the next Save runs again. |
| `network`         | Changes the Wi-Fi hotspot: on or off, its name, its password, and whether its name is hidden. It also scans for networks, forgets a saved one, sets the order of the saved ones, and passes Switch now and Cancel to the join. See [The Network module and the hotspot](#the-network-module-and-the-hotspot).                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                      |
| `network-join`    | Tests a Wi-Fi network under a NetworkManager checkpoint, comes back, counts down, and switches to it. See [The Wi-Fi join](#the-wi-fi-join).                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                       |

`SECRETS` in `tm-control/jobs/tm-job-set-secret` repeats the secrets' patterns (`VALUE_PATTERNS` in `core/secrets.py`) and restart units (`ENTERED` in `modules/secrets/router.py`), because the script imports nothing from tm-control; tests keep them the same.

## Status checks

`GET /api/v1/status` returns a report of check groups, which the Status page shows and the home page sums up in one line. Each module lists its groups in `Module.check_groups`, and the report shows them in `MODULES` order: Services, Apps, Configuration (the apps module's second group), Hardware, Network, Device (from the system module), and Date and time.

A check function takes a `Context` and returns a list of `Check`s, each with an `id`, a `title`, a `status` (`ok`, `warn`, `error`, or `unknown`), a one- or two-sentence `detail` that says what to do, and an optional `fix`:

| Fix kind  | The UI shows                                                                                                                                                                     |
| --------- | -------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- |
| `restart` | A button, for admins, that restarts `unit` after a confirmation. Make it with `restart_fix()` in `modules/services/units.py`, so every such button reads `Restart <unit title>`. |
| `rescan`  | One "Re-scan hardware" button at the end of the group, for admins, which calls `POST /status/rescan`.                                                                            |
| `link`    | A link to `href`, a page in the UI such as `/time` or `/device`.                                                                                                                 |
| `hint`    | `text`, after the detail.                                                                                                                                                        |

The runner in `core/checks.py` keeps the page up whatever a probe does:

- Checks never raise. A function that raises, or doesn't finish within the group's 5-second timeout, becomes one `unknown` check that names the exception class or the timeout, never its message, which could hold a command's output or a secret.
- All groups run at the same time, so a hung app costs about one timeout, not one per check.
- `Context.probe(key, fn)` runs `fn` once per report for every check that asks for the same key. Frigate's config and stats, Node-RED's status, `config.yml`, the unit states, and the bus listings are each read once.
- The report is cached for 5 seconds; `POST /status/rescan` (admins) runs it again at once.

Details name cameras, zones, radars, units, and config keys, never a URL, a password, or a command's output. The one exception is Frigate's log, which two checks quote:

- The Apps group's Frigate check is an error when `/api/config` says `safe_mode: true` (`probes.frigate_safe_mode`), which is how Frigate answers a config that doesn't validate: it starts with no cameras, so `config.cameras`, `config.zones`, `apps.frigate.cameras`, and `apps.go2rtc.streams` have nothing to compare, report `unknown`, and point at this check. The detail quotes Frigate's validation messages.
- The Configuration group's Frigate+ check (`config.frigate_plus`) reads `model.path` from Frigate's `config.yml` on disk, whether the `frigate_plus_api_key` secret is set, and whether a `plus://` model's two files are in `model_cache`. It warns about a key without a `plus://` model, and is an error for a `plus://` model Frigate can't get or can't use, quoting the log line that says why. Whenever Frigate doesn't answer, whatever systemd says of the unit (in a crash loop it's `active` between crashes), it quotes the traceback's last line without claiming the download caused it, because the journal's tail shows how Frigate stopped, not why; with no such line it's `unknown`. When that line holds Frigate's `Unable to refresh API token` (`REFUSED_KEY`), which Frigate raises for any answer but a token, the detail says Frigate+ gave no token for the key, as with a wrong key or an unreachable Frigate+, and links to the key form; both errors end with the ways out in `WAYS_OUT`. When the model's two files are on the device, Frigate loads it without asking Frigate+, so the detail quotes the line without the fetch advice and points at the Apps group's Frigate check. That check quotes the same line, with a link to the diagnostics and a pointer to the Services row's restart, since a crash loop without a `plus://` model has no other check to name its cause. `probes.frigate_journal` reads the current run's messages while the unit is active and either Frigate answers or systemd hasn't restarted it after a failure, and the journal's tail otherwise, where the run that failed left its traceback. A failure restart is `NRestarts` above 0 whose last automatic restart didn't follow Frigate's own exit 143 (`units.last_restart_cause`, from PID 1's journal, as the Services group reads it): after a Save & Restart the counter is 1 while Frigate starts, and the run before the save mustn't be quoted. One of Frigate's own restarts within `RESTART_LOOP_SPACING` (120 s) of the counted automatic restart before it is a loop, not a save (`units.restart_causes`, from PID 1's restart times alone; a hand restart resets the count, so a single restart is never a loop): the Services row warns with the counts, the Apps group's Frigate check says Frigate keeps stopping itself while it isn't answering, and the probe reads the tail. The restart Frigate's watchdog makes when a detector process dies is the known case; tm-control reads no log line for it.

Both quote only the `Message :` lines of Frigate's validation block and the last line of a traceback, through `redact()` in `modules/apps/checks.py`, which replaces anything shaped like a Frigate+ key with `<key>` and cuts each line to `MESSAGE_MAX` characters. `traceback_last_line` strips journalctl's prefix and the timestamp Frigate's s6 supervisor puts on each line (`S6_TIMESTAMP`) before it matches an exception line. It quotes nothing when s6's `[INFO] Service Frigate exited with code 0` line (`ORDERLY_EXIT`; a kill by SIGTERM counts too) comes after the last exception line. Frigate logs two tracebacks of its own while it stops for a Save & Restart, and the unit stays active until its container has halted, so the probe reads the run that is stopping; a crash of Frigate's own process has a nonzero exit line, so that crash loop still quotes; Frigate's watchdog restarts it the same way as a save when a detector process dies, so that loop quotes nothing, and is caught by its cadence instead.

The Hardware group's accelerator check claims only the host side ("Ready on the host and passed to Frigate"). Frigate's stats keep a dead detector process's pid and its starting 10.0 ms, so whether detection works is Frigate's to report, through the restarts above.

### Add a check

1. Write the function in the module's `checks.py`. Read through `context.probe` anything another check also reads, and run commands through `adapters/command.run` with an argv list, a timeout of at most 4 seconds, and an output cap. HTTP reads go to `127.0.0.1` only, with a 3-second timeout.
1. Add it to the module's `CheckGroup`, or make a new group and list it in the module's `check_groups`.
1. Test each status it can return, with synthetic data. The backend tests' `device_client` fixture builds the app as on a device (fake mode off, synthetic secrets, the test manifest), with the apps not answering and the hardware absent, so an API test runs the real code with only the outside world stubbed.
1. Add the check to `tests/fixtures/status_fake.json` if fake mode should show a new status or kind of fix.

### Node-RED's internal status

Node-RED answers `GET /tm-internal/status` on `127.0.0.1:1880` with its uptime, the errors from its last `config.yml` load, the database's schema version, and each radar's port and last reading. A flow on the `init-config` tab serves it. It checks the `X-TM-Internal-Token` header against `TM_INTERNAL_TOKEN` in `node-red-tm.env`, which the installer fills from the `node_red_internal_token` secret on every run, and refuses every request when that variable is unset or empty. `adapters/nodered.py` reads it, and calls the Location module's endpoints on the same port with the same token (see [The Location module](#the-location-module)). nginx answers 404 for `/nr/tm-internal/` in any letter case, because Node-RED matches paths whatever their case. The JSON fields are a contract between the flow and the checks: `script/tests/test_node_red_flows.py` and `tests/fixtures/nodered_status.json` pin them.

### The Detection module

The `detection` module serves the [Detection page](https://docs.trafficmonitor.ai/dev/use/detection/index.md). It reads Frigate's running config and `config.yml`, and the files in Frigate's `model_cache`. Its routes, under `/api/v1/models`:

| Route                           | Who                | What it does                                                                                                                                                |
| ------------------------------- | ------------------ | ----------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- |
| `GET /models`                   | Any logged-in user | The detector, the running model, the models in `model_cache` with their files, hashes, and each one's labels, and the two label lists for the running model |
| `PUT /models/upload/{filename}` | Admin              | Streams a model file, a sidecar, or a zip or tar.gz of both into `model_cache`                                                                              |
| `POST /models/{name}/sidecar`   | Admin              | Writes the sidecar for a model file that has none, from the form's values                                                                                   |
| `POST /models/{name}/use`       | Admin              | Sets Frigate's `model:` section to the model, then restarts Frigate                                                                                         |
| `POST /models/default/use`      | Admin              | Puts back the installer's model, or removes the section on a device without a Coral                                                                         |
| `GET /models/{name}/package`    | Admin              | A zip of the model's two files and `SHA256SUMS`                                                                                                             |
| `GET /models/{name}/file`       | Admin              | The model file alone, for a model with no sidecar to package, such as the installer's                                                                       |
| `DELETE /models/{name}`         | Admin              | Removes the model's files, unless it runs or is the installer's or Frigate's own default                                                                    |

The module writes only inside `model_cache` and Frigate's `config.yml`, plus its own state directory. Every `model_cache` write goes through a descriptor of the directory opened with `O_NOFOLLOW`, after `valid_name` has checked the name; `config.yml` is edited by its path through `RoundTripFile`, as `tm-control migrate` edits config files (a backup, an atomic replace, the owner kept). When Frigate answers in safe mode, which it enters when its config fails to validate, it runs a stand-in config, so `GET /models` reads the detector and the running model from `config.yml` and says `frigate_safe_mode`; a Use still goes through Frigate's API, which validates the whole config. The caps are 100 MB for a request and a model file, 2 MB for a sidecar, 3 archive members, and 512 MB of free storage left afterwards. Use goes through Frigate's config API, which checks the whole config, and edits `config.yml` itself, with a backup, only when Frigate doesn't answer. Both end in a restart of `frigate.service`.

Uploads need two things from the edge. nginx has its own location, `^~ /api/v1/models/upload/` in `tm-control-api.conf.j2`, with `client_max_body_size 100m` and `proxy_request_buffering off`, so the body streams to tm-control instead of being buffered. Because of that, tm-control reads the rest of a refused upload before it answers, so nginx can pass the answer on rather than a 502. The upload body is `application/octet-stream`, which the cross-site check in `core/csrf.py` admits along with `application/json`, because the check still requires a same-origin request. Every other `/api/` path keeps nginx's default body limit.

The sidecars are a Frigate+ model record's JSON. The module reads only the fields the page shows and keeps the whole file as it was uploaded, so a download returns it unchanged. It never puts a record's other fields in an answer, a log line, or an audit row.

### The Location module

The `location` module serves the [Location page](https://docs.trafficmonitor.ai/dev/use/location/index.md). It's for admins only, because the places hold exact coordinates: every route under `/api/v1/surveys` takes `require_admin`. The places are in `state.sqlite`; the place in use is also in Node-RED's `config.yml`, under `deployment:`, which is what Node-RED reads. tm-control never opens `tmdb.sqlite`, and Node-RED never opens `state.sqlite`.

| Route                                                                                   | What it does                                                                                                                                                                                                                                 |
| --------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- | -------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- |
| `GET /surveys`                                                                          | The place in use, the precision, the enabled sensors and their bearings, the places with Node-RED's usage counts, and the deployments recorded before any place. Runs the reconcile first.                                                   |
| `POST /surveys`, `PATCH` and `DELETE /surveys/{id}`                                     | Plan a place, edit a planned one, delete one that isn't in use                                                                                                                                                                               |
| `POST /surveys/{id}/deploy`                                                             | Writes the place and every enabled sensor's bearing into `config.yml`, then asks Node-RED every second, for up to 20 seconds, for the new deployments. `reloaded: false` when they didn't appear, which isn't an error: the file is written. |
| `PUT /surveys/precision`                                                                | Writes `database_precision`; with `round_stored`, also has Node-RED round the rows already stored                                                                                                                                            |
| `POST /surveys/{id}/location`, `POST /surveys/{id}/deployments/{deployment_id}/bearing` | Corrections: the place's point, re-rounded in Node-RED's rows, or one deployment's bearing; each records a row in `survey_corrections`                                                                                                       |
| `GET /surveys/{id}/deployments`, `GET /surveys/{id}/events`                             | A place's deployments, and its event count and span, from Node-RED                                                                                                                                                                           |
| `POST /surveys/import`                                                                  | Planned places from a CSV: a dry run lists what it read, and the import creates all or none                                                                                                                                                  |

The rules:

- `coordinates.py` holds them: survey ids (`<8 hex>-si`, from `secrets.token_hex(4)`), typed coordinates quantised to five decimal places half away from zero on their decimal text, and the stored ones rounded half away from zero, as SQLite's `ROUND` and the flows' `toFixed` do. The UI's `coordinates.ts` only checks a pasted pair before it sends; the API's answer wins.
- `config.py` edits `config.yml` through `RoundTripFile`, with `mapping_indent=4`, so comments, key order, and quoting stay. Each save keeps a backup beside the file, of which the newest 10 stay, and replaces it atomically. The backups of Frigate's `config.yml` from the Detection page's file fallback follow the same limit. Pruning touches only these `config.yml.<UTC stamp>.bak` names. It leaves the Ansible backups from `tmsetup.sh`, a copy made by hand, and every `<file>.<UTC stamp>.migrate.bak` from `tm-control migrate`, which can hold the only copy of what the migration removed. A file changed since it was read is a `ConcurrentEditError`, which the API answers with 409 `config_changed`.
- `reconcile.py` keeps the store and the file in step. It runs at claim, on every `GET /surveys`, and before the checks of every status report that isn't the cached one (`StatusCache`'s `prepare`), under `app.state.reconcile_lock`, which every write also holds. The status report waits at most two seconds for that lock, skips the run when a write holds it longer, and logs any error by its class name. Once per device it makes the first place: on a fresh device (no coordinates, no `survey_id`, and no backup), **First location** with no coordinates; on an upgraded one, a used place for each survey in the newest `tmdb-v0-*` or `tmdb-v1-*` backup in `node-red-tm/db/backup/`, opened read-only and immutable, then the place in use from the file. It waits until Node-RED reports schema version 2. An unreadable backup is skipped with one log line. Every run after that follows hand edits of the file, as [Edit the location by hand](https://docs.trafficmonitor.ai/dev/configuration/node-red-config/#edit-the-location-by-hand) describes.
- No coordinate, description, or reason is logged, audited, or put in an error message. Audit rows carry the survey id, and a deployment id or the precision.

The module calls six Node-RED endpoints, besides `/tm-internal/status`, on `127.0.0.1:1880` with `X-TM-Internal-Token`. Flows on the `init-config` tab serve them, and `script/tests/test_node_red_flows.py` pins them:
